question: An 18-year-old male is admitted with fever, headache and neck stiffness. He receives IV ceftriaxone. A lumbar puncture and culture of his cerebrospinal fluid reveal that the pathogenic organism is Neisseria meningitides. What is the appearance of this bacterium on gram staining?
explanation:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Neisseria species are gram-negative cocci. The bacteria cluster together in pairs to form diplococci. Other important gram-negative cocci include Moraxella catarrhalis and Haemophilus influenza.

Interpretation of gram stains for the non-microbiologist

Barenfanger and Drake. Laboratory medicine. 2001, number 7, vol 32

question: A 19-year-old woman is reviewed in the genitourinary medicine clinic. She presented with vaginal discharge and dysuria. Microscopy of an endocervical swab showed a Gram-negative coccus that was later identified as Neisseria gonorrhoea. This is her third episode of gonorrhoea in the past two years. What is the most likely complication from repeated infection?

A 42-year-old man attends with recurrent pneumonia. Following extensive investigation, he is diagnosed with HIV infection.

The patient is started on anti-viral combination therapy containing elvitegravir.

What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Bind to coreceptors necessary for HIV entrance into CD4+ cells
Binding to the catalytic site of the HIV protease, thereby preventing the cleavage of viral polyprotein precursors into mature, functional proteins
Block HIV reverse transcriptase thereby preventing the HIV virion from replicating
Inhibit reverse transcription by being incorporated into the growing viral DNA strand and preventing further addition of nucleotides
Prevents the integration of the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell
correctText: Prevents the integration of the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell
explanation:
Integrase inhibitors ('gravirs') - blocks the enzyme that inserts the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell

Prevents the integration of the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell

is correct. Elvitegravir, dolutegravir, and biktegravir are integrase inhibitors, which prevent the integration of the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell.

Bind to coreceptors necessary for HIV entrance into CD4+ cells

is incorrect. Entry inhibitors bind to coreceptors necessary for HIV entrance into CD4+ cells. Drugs in this class include maraviroc and enfuvirtide.

Block HIV reverse transcriptase thereby preventing the HIV virion from replicating

is incorrect. Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) bind to and block HIV reverse transcriptase thereby preventing the HIV virion from replicating. Drugs in this class include nevirapine and efavirenz.

Inhibit reverse transcription by being incorporated into the growing viral DNA strand and preventing further addition of nucleotides

is incorrect. Nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) inhibit reverse transcription by being incorporated into the growing viral DNA strand and preventing further addition of nucleotides. Drugs in this class include zidovudine (AZT), abacavir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, and tenofovir.

Binding to the catalytic site of the HIV protease, thereby preventing the cleavage of viral polyprotein precursors into mature, functional proteins

is incorrect. The antiretroviral protease inhibitors act by binding to the catalytic site of the HIV protease, thereby preventing the cleavage of viral polyprotein precursors into mature, functional proteins that are necessary for viral replication. Drugs in this class include indinavir, nelfinavir, and ritonavir.

question:
A 28-year-old lady is reviewed in a follow-up appointment at the sexual health clinic. Twelve months ago she was diagnosed with syphilis and was given intramuscular benzathine penicillin. Blood tests were taken a week prior to the follow-up appointment and the serology results are shown below:


TPHA	positive
VDRL	negative

What is the most likely explanation for the serology results shown above?
options: She has been re-infected and has developed syphilis
She has been successfully treated for syphilis
She has been suboptimally treated for syphilis
correctText: She has been successfully treated for syphilis
explanation:
Following treatment for syphilis: TPHA remains positive, VDRL becomes negative

VDRL becomes negative following treatment of syphilis. TPHA remains positive despite successful treatment of syphilis.

Her serology is consistent with previous syphilis infection, for example after successful treatment. Therefore 4 is the correct answer.

Options 1 and 5 suggest active infection with syphilis, in which case the VDRL would be positive.

Options 2 and 3 are causes of a false-positive VDRL test, which would not explain the negative VDRL but positive TPHA in the question.

question: A 34-year-old postman attends the Emergency Department following a dog bite to his right hand. What is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
explanation:
Animal bite - co-amoxiclav

A combination of doxycycline and metronidazole is recommended in the BNF if the patient is penicillin allergic

question:
A 36-year-old woman is brought into the emergency department by ambulance. Her family report that she collapsed at home, having been feeling unwell for several weeks with fatigue and intermittent abdominal pain. They have also noticed some darkening of the skin of her hands.

The patient has a history of menorrhagia and takes tranexamic acid at the time of menstruation. She has no known allergies, is a non-smoker and consumes no alcohol. There is a family history of diabetes and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB). She grew up in Pakistan and moved to the UK in 2004. Her family report that she also seems to have lost weight, but cannot quantify how much.

You ask the patient's family to leave to allow examination. Once they have left, the patient tells you that she has recently been diagnosed with TB and has been commenced on treatment by her local TB clinic, however, she does not know what medications she is currently taking or what sort of TB she has.

Urea and electrolyte results are demonstrated below:

Na+	125 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	6.0 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	13 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	2.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	60 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the most likely cause of this patient's acute deterioration?
explanation:
M. tuberculosis

This patient is most likely to have adrenal TB given her clinical history. Symptomatic anaemia would explain her fatigue, but not her electrolyte imbalance.

Rifampicin typically causes gastrointestinal upset, rashes and in severe cases hepatitis.

Isoniazid can cause gastrointestinal upset and hepatitis.

Addison's disease is hypoadrenalism resulting from autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands.

question:
A 42-year-old woman with a new diagnosis of HIV is discussing treatment with her consultant. Although she has a normal CD4 count, the consultant recommends commencing treatment with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The consultant recommends a backbone of emtricitabine and tenofovir and offers different options for the third drug. The patient and consultant decide to use dolutegravir as the third drug.

What is the mechanism of action of this third drug?
options: Binds directly to viral reverse transcriptase
Prevents synthesis of double-stranded viral DNA through chain termination
Prevents viral DNA from being inserted into the host genome
Negatively modulates the CCR5 chemokine co-receptor
correctText: Prevents viral DNA from being inserted into the host genome
explanation:
Integrase inhibitors ('gravirs') - blocks the enzyme that inserts the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell

The correct answer 'prevents viral DNA from being inserted into the host genome'.

Remembering the classes of HIV medications can be difficult so some mnemonics might help - but there are exceptions to most of these memory aides.

InTEGrase inhibitors have TEG in their name (raltegravir, elvitegravir, dolutegravir). They block the integrase enzyme which inserts the HIV viral genome into the DNA of the host cell. Integrase inhibitors prevent viral DNA from being inserted into the host genome.

Non nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) bind directly to viral reverse transcriptase. N

N

RTIs have an 'N' inserted in the middle, so they can be remembered as also having -vir- inserted in the middle of the word (ne

vir

apine, efa

vir

enz).

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) prevents synthesis of double-stranded viral DNA through chain termination. Many NRTIs end with 'ine'. Zidovudine, emtricitabine, didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine. Exceptions include abacavir and tenofovir. (Note that nevirapine also ends in -ine but is an NNRTI). NRTIs are a common backbone of HAART for HIV.

Protease inhibitors prevent viral replication by binding directly to viral protease. These end in 'navir' (indinavir, nelfinavir, ritonavir, saquinavir).

CCR5 fusion inhibitors negatively modulate the CCR5 chemokine co-receptor. These include maraviroc and enfuvirtide. HIV uses CCR5 and/or CXCR4 as a co-receptor to enter T cells.

question:
A 42-year-old man with a known HIV infection presents with progressively worsening speech difficulties, behavioural changes, and impaired coordination over the past two months. He is not on antiretroviral therapy.

On examination, there is evidence of dysarthria and ataxia.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals multifocal, non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect or surrounding oedema.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A patient who is known to have HIV presents gradually worsening speech and behavioural problems associated with coordination difficulties. A MRI shows multifocal non-enhancing lesions - JC virus

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

is the correct diagnosis, as the clinical presentation aligns with this condition. PML is caused by the reactivation of the JC virus in individuals with compromised immune systems, particularly those with HIV and CD4 counts below 200 cells/µL. The disease manifests with progressive neurological symptoms, including alterations in speech and behaviour, motor deficits, and ataxia. Characteristic MRI findings include multifocal non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect, indicative of demyelination secondary to JC virus infection. The patient's clinical presentation and radiological findings are typical for PML.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis

is not the appropriate diagnosis in this case. While it is a common opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV (CD4 < 100 cells/µL), its clinical manifestations usually involve focal neurological deficits such as hemiparesis, seizures, or confusion. MRI typically reveals ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding oedema, often located in the basal ganglia or cortical areas. The absence of enhancing lesions coupled with speech and behavioural changes without evidence of mass effect renders toxoplasmosis an unlikely diagnosis for this patient.

CMV encephalitis

can present with confusion, lethargy, and seizures in patients with profound immunosuppression (CD4 < 50 cells/µL). Neuroimaging often reveals periventricular white matter hyperintensities with associated enhancement and possible ventriculitis, findings not observed in this patient. The absence of characteristic periventricular involvement and ventriculitis on MRI makes CMV encephalitis less likely.

Cryptococcal meningitis

does not correspond to this diagnosis; it represents a frequent fungal infection among immunocompromised individuals, including those with advanced HIV infection. Its hallmark symptoms include headache, fever, photophobia, and mental status changes rather than focal neurological signs or progressive motor dysfunction like ataxia observed here. MRI scans may be normal or show nonspecific findings such as meningeal enhancement which are absent in this patient's imaging studies. The described white matter lesions do not match those seen in cryptococcal infections.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL)

should also be discounted; PCNSL is a high-grade B-cell lymphoma that occurs predominantly in individuals experiencing severe HIV immunosuppression (CD4 < 50 cells/µL). Clinical features commonly include focal neurological deficits, altered mental state, and seizures. On MRI scans PCNSL presents as enhancing lesions that may be solitary or multiple accompanied by oedema and mass effects on MRI scans. The lack of these characteristic features on the patient's MRI makes PCNSL an improbable diagnosis for this case.

question:
A 28-year-old man presents to his GP with a painless ulcer on his penis which has been present for several weeks. He otherwise has no symptoms and is generally well in himself. On examination, he also has non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.

The GP prescribes penicillin. Several hours later, the patient presents to the Emergency Department with fever and a new rash. On examination, he appears well but has marked flushing of his torso. There is good air entry on auscultation, with no wheeze. Observations are as follows:


Heart rate: 98 beats/min
Respiratory rate: 18 breaths/min
Blood pressure: 132/72 mmHg
Temperature: 37.9ºC

What is the most appropriate next step in management, given the likely explanation?
explanation:
The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, unlike an anaphylactic reaction, will not present with hypotension and wheeze

The correct answer is oral paracetamol. The patient initially presented with features of syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection that is increasing in incidence in the UK. He had classic findings of a painless penile ulcer and non-tender localised lymphadenopathy. The GP then commenced management with penicillin. It is key to note here that the patient did not then present with an anaphylactic reaction to penicillin - he appeared well on examination, with normal auscultation and no hypotension. He instead presented with the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which is sometimes seen following treatment of syphilis, thought to be due to the release of endotoxins. It presents as fever, rash and tachycardia, but there is crucially no wheeze and no hypotension. No treatment is required except for antipyretics, if needed.

Intramuscular adrenaline would be used if anaphylaxis were suspected. We have no reason to suspect this here, given the stable observations and good air entry.

Chlorphenamine is an antihistamine and would also be given as part of the anaphylaxis protocol, to prevent further symptoms. Anaphylaxis is unlikely as the patient is well.

An intravenous corticosteroid, such as hydrocortisone, would also be given as part of the anaphylaxis protocol.

Loratadine is another antihistamine, taken orally, often over-the-counter for the management of simple conditions such as allergic rhinitis and mild urticaria. It does not play a role here.

question:
A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a fever and yellow skin and eyes. He has recently had an illness characterized by fever, chills, headache, and myalgia after returning from Angola. He seemed to recover from the illness and was well for a period of 48 hours before deteriorating. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and is on tocilizumab.

On examination, there is bleeding from his eyes and mucus membranes and he is visibly jaundiced. The temperature is 38.5ºC.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Yellow fever typically presents with flu like illness → brief remission→ followed by jaundice and haematemesis

Yellow fever

is the correct answer. The patient presents with a flu-like illness after returning from Angola, followed by a brief period of remission with subsequent recrudescence of fever and the development of jaundice and haemorrhage from the eyes and mucus membranes. This presentation is typical of yellow fever (and the brief period of remission is characteristic). Tocilizumab treatment for rheumatoid arthritis means the yellow fever vaccine is contraindicated and would put the patient at increased risk of developing the illness.

Ebola

is incorrect. This is a cause of viral hemorrhagic fever and can cause flu-like symptoms and subsequent jaundice and hemorrhagic complications. However, a period of remission before the recrudescence of the disease is not typical. Furthermore, Angola has never had an ebola outbreak but yellow fever is endemic. In this context, this diagnosis is less likely.

Lassa fever

is incorrect. This is another viral hemorrhagic fever that can result in fever and bleeding from mucus membranes. However, it is mainly endemic in West Africa and unlikely to be found in Angola.

Malaria

is incorrect. This is of course the common cause of fever in the returning traveller. It is said that the three most common causes of fever in returning travellers are malaria, malaria, and malaria! However, this is unlikely to cause hemorrhagic complications in contrast to yellow fever and therefore is less likely in this case.

Typhoid

is incorrect. This is another one of the three most common causes of fever in the returning traveller. It is typified by fever, myalgia, and constipation. Bleeding complications are not expected and so this is less likely.

question: A 22-year-old female presents with an offensive vaginal discharge. History and examination findings are consistent with a diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Advice regarding hygiene and cotton underwear
explanation:
Bacterial vaginosis: oral metronidazole

The correct answer is

Oral metronidazole

. Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a polymicrobial clinical syndrome resulting from replacement of the normal hydrogen peroxide producing

Lactobacillus

sp. in the vagina with high concentrations of anaerobic bacteria, such as

Gardnerella vaginalis

,

Mycoplasma hominis

, and others. The first-line treatment for BV according to UK guidelines is oral metronidazole 400mg twice daily for 5-7 days.

Oral azithromycin

is incorrect because it's an antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections including sexually transmitted infections like Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, but not typically used for BV.

Topical hydrocortisone

is also incorrect. It's a corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation and irritation but does not treat the underlying infection caused by BV.

Clotrimazole pessary

is another incorrect option. Clotrimazole is an antifungal medication primarily used to treat yeast infections such as Candida albicans, not bacterial infections like BV.

Lastly, while providing

advice regarding hygiene and cotton underwear

can be beneficial in preventing further irritation or potential infections, it does not address the active infection of BV itself which requires antimicrobial therapy. Therefore, this option is also incorrect.

question:
A 28-year-old student is admitted out of hours to the infectious diseases ward with suspected malaria following a backpacking trip around South East Asia. Malarial films are as follows:


Thick film	Parasite burden of 1.5%
Thin film	Non-falciparum malaria - Looks like Plasmodium knowlesi

On admission, the patient is systemically well with observations at follows:

HR	90bpm
BP	123/75 mmHg
RR	16 breaths per minute
Oxygen Sats	97% on air
Temp	36.4º

Although being relatively well on first admission, you are called to review her overnight a few hours later, due to her condition worsening. You arrive to find her observations as follows:

HR	110bpm
BP	105/65 mmHg
RR	25 breaths per minute
Oxygen Sats	93% on air
Temp	38.4º

Which of the following attributes make Plasmodium knowlesi infections particularly dangerous?
options: Slow growth leading to late presentation
explanation:
P. knowlesi

Plasmodium sp.

have two reproductive cycles; an exo-erythrocytic cycle which occurs in hepatocytes, and an erythrocytic cycle which occurs in the red blood cells. The length of the erythrocytic cycle varies from species to species, with

P. knowlesi

having the fastest cycle at around 24 hours. The end stage in the cycle involves lysis of the red cells and release of additional parasites, meaning that

P. knowlesi

is capable of producing very high parasite counts in a short space of time.

For this reason, in

Plasmodium knowlesi

infection, severe parasitaemia should be defined as >1%, whereas in other species, >2% is a marker of severe parasitaemia.

In regards to other options,

Plasmodium ovale

and

Plasmodium vivax

can form hypnozoites, causing clinical infection long after patients leave malarial areas. Cytoadherence is an attribute displayed by red cells infected by

Plasmodium falciparum

parasites.

question:
A 24-year-old man attends the clinic with concerns that he may have contracted HIV. He states that he had unprotected anal sex with a male partner 3 weeks ago. He is asymptomatic.

What diagnostic test is recommended?
explanation:
Combined HIV antibody/antigen tests are now the first-line test for HIV screening of asymptomatic individuals or patients with signs and symptoms of chronic infection

HIV 1/2 antigen/antibody combination test

is correct. This fourth-generation assay should be used to screen individuals for HIV as it will detect HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies (Ab) and antigens (Ag) with high sensitivity within a short window period (technically still 45 days as per BHIVA guidelines).

CD4 count

is incorrect. Once the diagnosis of HIV is confirmed, CD4 levels should be checked for prognostication and to assess the risk of infective and malignant complications.

HIV-1 NAAT

is incorrect. If the initial screening results are not reactive or indeterminate and acute HIV infection is suspected then HIV-1 NAAT or p24 testing should be considered. PCR testing is the most common method of NAAT. HIV RNA becomes detectable by NAAT in plasma approximately 10 days after infection. HIV NAAT assays offer very little advantage over fourth-generation assays in terms of earlier detection of acute infection and are not recommended for initial HIV screening as they may also give false positive results.

P24

is incorrect. One distinctive HIV antigen is a viral protein called p24, a structural protein that makes up most of the HIV viral core, or 'capsid'. High levels of p24 are present in the blood serum of newly infected individuals during the short period between infection and seroconversion, making p24 antigen assays useful in diagnosing primary HIV infection. If the initial screening results are not reactive or indeterminate and acute HIV infection is suspected then HIV-1 NAAT or p24 testing should be considered.

Western blot (lysate)

is incorrect. The HIV Western blot is an enzyme immunoassay for the in-vitro detection of antibodies to HIV in human serum or plasma. It is intended as a more specific confirmation test on blood or plasma specimens found repeatedly reactive using a screening procedure. It is not recommended for screening.

question: A 31-year-old man from Russia who is known to be HIV positive presents with purple plaques on his skin. Which of the following viruses is thought to be the cause of Kaposi's sarcoma?
explanation:
Kaposi's sarcoma - caused by HHV-8 (human herpes virus 8)

The correct answer is

HHV-8

. Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that forms from the cells lining lymph or blood vessels. It is caused by the human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). The virus is found in the lesions of all patients with KS. HHV-8 infection alone, however, isn't sufficient to cause KS; immunosuppression plays a key role in its pathogenesis. This explains why it's most often seen in people with HIV/AIDS.

HTLV-1

, or Human T-cell leukemia virus type 1, does not cause Kaposi's sarcoma. HTLV-1 is linked primarily to adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma and HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis.

HIV-2

is incorrect because it refers to a type of HIV that weakens the immune system by destroying important cells that fight disease and infection, but it does not directly cause Kaposi's sarcoma. However, like HIV-1, it can make an individual more susceptible to other infections such as HHV-8.

The option

CMV

, or Cytomegalovirus, is also incorrect. While CMV can cause illness in people with weakened immune systems and can be reactivated in HIV-positive individuals, it doesn't directly lead to Kaposi's Sarcoma.

Lastly,

HPV-8

, or Human papillomavirus 8, does not cause Kaposi's Sarcoma either. HPV types are associated with various cancers such as cervical cancer and head and neck cancers but not specifically with Kaposi's Sarcoma.

question: A patient who was an intravenous drug user in the 1990s asks for a hepatitis C test. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Refer him for pre-test counselling to discuss the pros and cons of testing
Advise him that no accurate test is currently available but that he should undertake normal precautions
Refer him to gastroenterology for a liver biopsy

question:
A 24-year-old heterosexual man presents to GUM with a history of dysuria, urethral irritation and milky discharge from the urethra. Urethral microscopy reveals >10 polynuclear lymphocytes per field but no gonorrhoea is seen and urine dip is normal. He did a home test 3 days ago when his symptoms started and Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea NAATs were negative. His urine dipstick is normal. His last sexual encounter was 3 weeks ago. You make a clinical diagnosis of non specific urethritis (NSU).

What is the most appropriate action to take?
options: Reassure the patient; his symptoms will resolve spontaneously
Tell the patient to repeat his Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea tests in 2 weeks' time.
Refer to urology for their assessment and opinion
explanation:
Non specific (non gonococcal) urethritis is a common presentation where inflammatory cells but no gonococcal bacteria are seen on swab; it requires treatment with doxycycline or azithromycin

The presence of pus cells on urethral swab suggests a diagnosis of non-specific urethritis, which commonly presents with symptoms similar to these. BASHH recommend treating with oral doxycycline. The window period for

Chlamydia

and

Gonorrhoea

tests is generally 2 weeks so the home test he did is likely to be accurate; while retesting may be appropriate it should not delay treatment, and should not be delayed further.

As there is no evidence of gonococcal bacteria on microscopy there is no indication to treat as

Gonorrhoea

. There is no current indication to refer to Urology and no current reason to treat the patient for HSV.

question: A health care assistant sustains a needlestick injury whilst taking blood from a patient who is known to be HIV positive. Following thorough washing of the wound what is the most appropriate management?
options: HIV test of health care worker in 3 months to determine treatment
Immediate p24 HIV test of health care worker to determine treatment
explanation:
Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV: oral antiretroviral therapy for 4 weeks

The correct answer is

Oral antiretroviral therapy for 4 weeks

. According to UK guidelines, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) should be started as soon as possible after a needlestick injury from an HIV-positive patient. This usually involves a combination of three oral antiretroviral drugs for four weeks. The aim is to prevent the establishment of HIV infection in the exposed healthcare worker.

Discussing the other options:

HIV test of health care worker in 3 months to determine treatment

is incorrect because it delays potential treatment. While it's true that antibodies to HIV often don't appear until several weeks after exposure and testing at three months can detect these antibodies, waiting this long could allow an infection to become established if PEP is not given immediately after exposure.

Immediate p24 HIV test of health care worker to determine treatment

is also not accurate. An immediate p24 antigen test would only detect an existing infection in the healthcare worker, not a new infection from the needlestick injury. Furthermore, this would not guide the need for immediate post-exposure prophylaxis which should be initiated regardless of this result.

Oral antiretroviral therapy for 3 months

is incorrect because it extends beyond the recommended duration. UK guidelines suggest four weeks of PEP following a high-risk exposure such as a needlestick injury from an HIV-positive patient.

Lastly,

Intravenous zidovudine

is not recommended as first-line management for occupational exposures like needlestick injuries. Oral antiretroviral therapy has been shown to be effective and has largely replaced intravenous routes due its ease of administration and good patient compliance. Intravenous zidovudine may be used in certain situations but typically only when oral administration isn't possible or when higher drug levels are needed.

question: A 34-year-old man from Zimbabwe is admitted with abdominal pain to the Emergency Department. An abdominal x-ray reveals urinary bladder calcification. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Schistosoma

Schistosomiasis is the most common cause of bladder calcification worldwide

question: A 87 year old lady presents to the Emergency Department with a two day history of new confusion. Her heart rate is 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 95/45 mmHg and temperature 38.4ºC. You suspect urinary sepsis and after taking urine and blood cultures you start appropriate treatment with intravenous fluids and broad spectrum antibiotics. Later that day the microbiology lab phones to inform you the microscopy of the urine sample shows Gram positive cocci in clusters. What is the likely organism in this case?

A 34-year-old woman presents with fatigue and weight loss. She admits to having intermittent abdominal pain and nausea but no vomiting or loose stools. She was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis three years ago, took medications for three months, and prematurely stopped taking them.

On examination, she appears slim. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg when sitting and 90/60 mmHg when standing. Blood results are as follows:


Na+	128 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	5.8 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	4 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	75 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the next best investigation to determine the underlying cause?
explanation:
M. tuberculosis

The most appropriate answer is

serum cortisol

. The patient's history of tuberculosis, non-compliance with treatment, symptoms of fatigue and weight loss, and postural hypotension with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia suggest the possibility of adrenal insufficiency. This can occur as a result of adrenal tuberculosis, which may have developed due to her discontinuation of anti-TB therapy. The most appropriate next step would be to check her serum cortisol levels to confirm or exclude this diagnosis. Other investigations listed may be relevant for different clinical scenarios but are less likely in this case based on the information provided.

Faecal calprotectin

levels increase in cases of intestinal inflammation, which includes mainly inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Patients with IBD present with fatigue and weight loss; however, they will also have a history of diarrhoea, which may be associated with blood. Since this patient has no history of diarrhoea, IBD is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

Liver function tests

would not help in arriving at the cause of her symptoms. Typical clinical features of liver disease, such as jaundice and itching, are not present, and liver disease would not explain the postural hypotension and hyperkalaemia in this case.

Since this patient presents with unintentional weight loss,

thyroid function tests

could be considered, with hyperthyroidism as a differential. However, other typical symptoms of hyperthyroidism, such as heat intolerance, increased appetite, palpitations or tremors, are not mentioned in the scenario, making this less likely.

Performing an

ultrasound of the abdomen

can be done in patients presenting with abdominal pain. However, this patient has vague symptoms, and blood tests indicate electrolyte imbalances, which suggests adrenal insufficiency. CT scanning is preferred for adrenal imaging as ultrasonographic visualisation of the adrenals is difficult due to their posterior location within the abdomen. Adrenal imaging would typically be done after biochemical confirmation of adrenal insufficiency (with a serum cortisol test), not as a first-line investigation.

question:
A 32-year-old man attends with a fever. There are no localising features during the systematic enquiry or examination. He recently completed chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma. Observations are as follows: heart rate 105 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, blood pressure 135/75 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on air, and temperature 38.1ºC. The patient has a Hickman line in situ.

Blood results are as follows:


Neuts	0.2 * 10 9/L	(2.0 - 7.0)

The microbiologist calls the following day to advise that an organism has grown from peripheral blood cultures.

What organism has most likely been cultured?
explanation:
Most common organism found in central line infections -

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is correct. This patient has neutropenic sepsis, a potentially life-threatening complication of chemotherapy. In this case, the Hickman line is a potential source of infection.

Staphylococcus epidermidis

, which is coagulase-negative, is a common cause of central line infections.

Candida albicans

is incorrect. Systemic candidiasis is an important complication in neutropenic patients and those undergoing treatment for cancer. This infection has increased persistently over the past three decades and represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality among high-risk individuals. However, it is much rarer in comparison to gram-positive bacteraemia.

Enterococcus faecium

is incorrect. A progressive increase in infections with multi-drug resistant

Enterococcus faecium

(e.g. vancomycin resistance Enterococcus) has been reported, especially in cancer patients and neutropenic patients. This is potentially driven by selection pressures from broad-spectrum antibiotic use. However, it remains a relatively rare cause of bacteraemias in comparison to

Staphylococcus epidermidis

.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

is incorrect.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

has historically been one of the major causes of severe sepsis and death among neutropenic cancer patients. Therefore all patients with prolonged neutropaenia should be on a prophylactic antibiotic which has anti-Pseudomonal cover (e.g. ciprofloxacin). However, this type of infection is very rare in comparison to

Staphylococcus epidermidis

.

Staphylococcus aureus

is incorrect. This is another common cause of infections in neutropenic patients, again most likely secondary to indwelling lines. However, it is less common than coagulase-negative gram-positive infections.

question: A patient with HIV is reviewed. Which one of the following is an example of a nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitors?
explanation:
HIV drugs, rule of thumb:

The correct answer is

Zidovudine

. Zidovudine, also known as AZT, is a nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). NRTIs are a class of antiretroviral drugs used in the treatment of HIV infection. They work by inhibiting the action of reverse transcriptase, an enzyme that HIV uses to replicate its genetic material within a host cell. By doing so, they prevent the virus from multiplying and can reduce the amount of virus in the body.

Indinavir

is not a nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor but rather a protease inhibitor. Protease inhibitors work differently than NRTIs; they block another enzyme that HIV needs to make copies of itself called protease. By blocking this enzyme, they prevent the virus from producing new virus particles.

Ritonavir

, like indinavir, is also a protease inhibitor and works in much the same way. It's often used in combination with other protease inhibitors to boost their effectiveness due to its ability to inhibit cytochrome P450 3A4 enzymes which metabolise most protease inhibitors.

Ribavirin

is an antiviral medication but it does not belong to the class of NRTIs either. It's primarily used for the treatment of hepatitis C and some viral haemorrhagic fevers. Its mechanism of action isn't fully understood but it's thought to interfere with duplication of viral genetic material.

Finally,

Efavirenz

is not an NRTI but rather a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). While NNRTIs also inhibit reverse transcriptase, they do so differently than NRTIs. Rather than mimicking the building blocks that HIV uses to create DNA copies (as NRTIs do), NNRTIs bind directly to reverse transcriptase and disrupt its function.

question:
A 22-year-old woman presents with lethargy, pyrexia and headaches. She is a student and returned from a holiday in Ibiza ten days ago. These symptoms have been present for the past six days and she is wondering whether she may need an antibiotic. She also has a history of menorrhagia and is concerned that she may be anaemic. Clinical examination reveals a temperature of 37.9ºC and marked cervical lymphadenopathy. You order a full blood count which is reported as follows:


Hb	12.1 g/dl
Platelets	189 * 109/l
WCC	13.1 * 109/l
Neutrophils	5.2 * 109/l
Lymphocytes	6.2 * 109/l
Film	Atypical lymphocytes seen

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Septicaemia secondary to streptococcal throat infection
explanation:
Atypical lymphocytes - ?glandular fever

The correct answer is

infectious mononucleosis

. This patient presents with typical symptoms of infectious mononucleosis, including fever, fatigue, headache, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Additionally, the blood film shows atypical lymphocytes which can be seen in infectious mononucleosis. The disease is commonly caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and often affects young adults.

The first incorrect option is

acute lymphoblastic leukemia

. While this condition may present with similar symptoms such as fever and fatigue, the blood count findings are not consistent with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. In this case, we would expect to see a higher white cell count with a predominance of blast cells.

The second incorrect option is

Hashimoto's thyroiditis

. This autoimmune thyroid disorder typically presents with hypothyroidism symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. Although Hashimoto's thyroiditis can cause an enlarged thyroid gland that could potentially lead to cervical lymphadenopathy, the presence of pyrexia and atypical lymphocytes on blood film make this diagnosis less likely.

The third incorrect option is

HIV seroconversion

. HIV seroconversion can present with flu-like symptoms including fever and lymphadenopathy; however, the presence of atypical lymphocytes in the blood film is more suggestive of infectious mononucleosis. Furthermore, there is no mention of any high-risk behaviour or recent unprotected sexual encounters that might suggest an increased risk for HIV infection.

Lastly,

septicaemia secondary to streptococcal throat infection

is also an incorrect option. Although streptococcal throat infections can cause fever and cervical lymphadenopathy, septicaemia would typically present with a much higher temperature and systemic signs of sepsis such as tachycardia or hypotension. Moreover, the presence of atypical lymphocytes on blood film is not typical for a streptococcal infection.

question: A 23-year-old woman comes for review. She has had recurrent genital warts for the past 4 years which have failed to respond to topical podophyllum. On one occasion she had cryotherapy but will not have it again due to local discomfort. On examination she has a large number of fleshy genital warts around her introitus. What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

A 28-year-old man presents with fever, headache and myalgia. He has no significant past medical history. He works as a sewage treatment plant worker. On examination, he is febrile with mild conjunctival suffusion without discharge. There is no rash, jaundice, or evidence of organ dysfunction.

What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
Leptospirosis - give oral doxycycline or azithromycin for mild-moderate disease

This patient presents with features consistent with

leptospirosis,

a zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Leptospira species. Transmission most commonly occurs through direct or indirect contact with the urine of infected animals—especially rats—or via contaminated water or soil, which is particularly relevant given his occupation in sewage treatment. Early symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, and the characteristic finding of conjunctival suffusion. For mild to moderate cases of leptospirosis, oral doxycycline is considered the first-line treatment. It is effective in reducing the duration of symptoms and preventing complications. Such cases are generally managed on an outpatient basis unless there are signs suggesting severe disease.

Prescribe intravenous benzylpenicillin

is not appropriate in this scenario. Intravenous benzylpenicillin is reserved for severe leptospirosis (such as Weil’s disease), which may present with jaundice, renal impairment, haemorrhage, or haemodynamic instability. This patient does not exhibit any features of severe disease; therefore, intravenous antibiotics are not indicated at this time.

Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin

is also not recommended. Although some evidence exists for its efficacy in leptospirosis, ciprofloxacin is less effective than doxycycline or penicillin-based regimens and is not routinely used as first-line therapy according to most guidelines.

Prescribe intravenous ceftriaxone

would not be appropriate here either. Ceftriaxone may be used in cases of severe leptospirosis or when oral therapy cannot be tolerated (for example, due to vomiting). However, given that this patient has a mild presentation and can tolerate oral medication, doxycycline remains the preferred option.

Prescribe oral paracetamol

is incorrect. While paracetamol can help alleviate symptoms such as fever and myalgia, antibiotic therapy is required even in mild cases to reduce the risk of progression and complications from leptospirosis. Prescribing paracetamol without antibiotics would risk undertreating a potentially serious infection.

question:
A 27-year-old student presents to the GP with a 24-hour history of explosive diarrhoea and vomiting. On further questioning, he has not noticed any blood in his stool, has no history of foreign travel. He tells you he has been eating rice kept warm in a rice cooker for several days.

What is the likely pathogenic organism underlying his symptoms?
explanation:
Bacillus cereus

This young gentleman is likely to have toxigenic food poisoning from

Bacillus cereus

.

Bacillus cereus

spores germinate in cooked rice and produce toxin if the cooked product is kept insufficiently chilled.

S. aureus

will also cause a toxigenic food poisoning but the specific history in this case makes this a less likely underlying organism. Equally Norwalk virus can cause explosive diarrhoea and vomiting but is not associated with any specific food stuffs.

Campylobacter

and

Shigella

cause bacterial food poisoning and would likely have a longer history with bloody diarrhoea.

question:
A 29-year-old woman presents to a sexual health clinic with a thin, white vaginal discharge which she reports has a foul, fish-like odour. The patient reports multiple sexual partners without using barrier protection.

Diagnostic testing is performed and microscopy confirms the presence of clue cells, the vaginal pH is found to be 4.6 and a whiff test is positive.

What organism is predominately responsible for this patient's presentation?
explanation:
Bacterial vaginosis - overgrowth of predominately

This patient has presented with features of bacterial vaginosis, a condition caused by excess growth of predominately anaerobic, non-lactobacilli organisms, the most common of which is

Gardnerella vaginalis

. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with a white/grey, 'fishy' offensive-smelling discharge and diagnosis is on confirmation of a higher than normal vaginal pH (above 4.5), the presence of clue cells on microscopy and/or a positive whiff test.

Candida albicans

is a fungal organism and the most common cause of vaginal candidiasis, also known as thrush. Patients often present with a whitish, 'cottage cheese-like' discharge and severe itching/burning of the vagina or vulva. Although the fungus may be present in bacterial vaginosis it is far less common than other organisms.

Escherichia coli

is the commonest organism found in the aerobic counterpart of bacterial vaginosis, aerobic vaginitis. Patient general present with a thin reddish, odourless discharge and a high vaginal pH. The condition can progress resulting in extensive erosions or ulcerations.

Healthy vaginal microbiota consists mainly of lactobacilli with

Lactobacillus acidophilus

being the commonest. Bacterial vaginosis is due to an excessive overgrowth of other organisms and is characterised by a decline in lactobacilli.

Trichomonas vaginalis

is an anaerobic, flagellated parasite that causes trichomoniasis, a frequently asymptomatic sexually transmitted disease. Again, although

T. vaginalis

may be present in bacterial vaginosis, it is much less prominent when compared to other organisms.

question:
A 68-year-old man presents having returned home from a holiday in South Africa with a 4-day history of coryzal-like symptoms, fever and a dry cough.

He has a past medical history of mild asthma and moderate eczema. He is on a beclomethasone inhaler and a topical corticosteroid.

Investigation results are shown below:


Hb	120	(115 - 160 g/L)
WBC	16 * 10 9	(4.0 - 11.0 /L)
Platelets	180 * 10 9	(150 - 400 /L)
Na+	131	136–146 mmol/L
K+	4.0	3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine	110	53–106 μmol/L
Amylase	120	25–125 U/L
AST	50	12–38 U/L


ECG	sinus bradycardia, 54 bpm
Chest x-ray	bilateral mid to lower zone consolidation

What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Bilateral, mid-to-lower zone patchy consolidation in an older patient → ?

The patient's presentation is indicative of Legionnaires' disease with several notable findings pointing towards

legionella pneumophila

as the most likely causative organism. The organism is typically found in water tanks, and therefore patients are often exposed from such facilities found in hotels or spas when travelling abroad on holiday. The presence of hyponatraemia is a characteristic feature of Legionnaires' disease, reflecting the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion often associated with this condition and the deranged liver function tests could also be attributed to Legionella-induced hepatic involvement. Sinus bradycardia on the ECG is a recognised manifestation of Legionella pneumonia as well as the bilateral mid to lower zone consolidation observed on chest X-ray.

Klebsiella pneumonia

is less likely as the causative organism in this case due to several factors. Firstly,

Klebsiella pneumonia

typically affects the upper lobes of the lungs and is unilateral, unlike this patient's chest X-ray. Additionally, hyponatraemia, liver impairment and bradycardia are not commonly associated with the condition. Alcoholism is a known risk factor for Klebsiella pneumonia, but it is not mentioned in the patient's medical history.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

(TB) is less likely as the causative organism in this case for several reasons. Although TB is endemic in South Africa, the patient's clinical presentation is not consistent with TB infection. TB typically manifests with a more chronic and insidious onset of symptoms, unlike the acute onset observed in this patient shortly after returning from South Africa. Additionally, the presence of bradycardia and the specific bilateral mid to lower zone consolidation observed on chest X-ray are not typical features of TB.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae

is less likely as the causative organism in this case due to discrepancies in the patient's clinical presentation. While

Mycoplasma pneumoniae

infections are present in South Africa, the presence of bradycardia and the specific bilateral mid to lower zone consolidation observed on chest X-ray are not consistent with typical features of this infection.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae

infections typically do not result in bradycardia, and the chest X-ray findings usually include patchy infiltrates or interstitial changes rather than the bilateral consolidation seen in this patient.

Plasmodium falciparum

is unlikely as the causative organism in this case for several reasons. Firstly, the patient's clinical presentation of respiratory symptoms, fever, and abnormal laboratory findings is not consistent with malaria caused by

Plasmodium falciparum

. Malaria typically presents with symptoms such as fever, chills, headache, and myalgia, but respiratory symptoms and bilateral mid to lower zone consolidation on chest X-ray are not typical features. Additionally, the patient's recent travel history to South Africa, where malaria transmission is relatively low, further diminishes the likelihood of

Plasmodium falciparum

infection.

question:
A young black African male recently moved from Zimbabwe presents with a skin lesion on his hand. On examination you note an ulceration with a black centre (eschar) with surrounding oedema, he says it is not painful.

What is an important microbe to consider?
explanation:
Painless black eschar - anthrax

Classical description of a cutaneous manifestation of anthrax, caused by

Bacillus anthracis

. Zimbabwe had the largest known outbreak of more than 10,000 cases in the late 80's (Central African Journal of Medicine, 1996)

Mycobacterium ulcerans

usually presents as a painless nodule and progresses to an ulcer without an eschar.

Strongyloides stercoralis

is an helminth which is contracted through contact with soil containing the larvae and most commonly in the tropics and subtropics. Usually asymptomatic and raised eosinophils maybe the only indication.

Chikungunya virus is contracted through infected mosquitos. Commonly present with myalgia, arthralgia and fevers.

Mycobacterium leprae

causes leprosy characterised by damages to peripheral nerves, skin and muscle.

question:
A 19-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit with a 3-day history of a generalised headache and photophobia. There is a history of nausea but no vomiting and he complains of intense body aches. He has a past medical history of type 1 diabetes and has no allergies.

On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic. His peripheries are cool. Chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Kernig's sign is positive.

Ceftriaxone 2g is administered.

CSF analysis:


Opening pressure	25 cmH20	10-20 cmH20
White blood cells	> 100 cells/µL (polymorphonuclear leucocytes)	0-5 cells/µL
Protein	1.1 g/L	0.15-0.45
Glucose	1.5 mmol/L	2.8-4.2 mmol/L

Which of the following should be given alongside the current treatment?
explanation:
Dexamethasone improves outcomes (by reducing neurological sequelae) in the treatment of bacterial meningitis

This patient has bacterial meningitis as indicated from the CSF analysis. NICE guidelines recommend treating bacterial meningitis with dexamethasone if lumbar puncture reveals either: purulent CSF, white cell count > 1000 cells/µL, raised white cell count plus protein count > 1g/L, or bacteria on gram stain. Dexamethasone should be given within 4 hours of starting antibiotics and should be avoided if the duration from starting antibiotics is beyond 12 hours.

Aciclovir is indicated to treat a viral meningitis. It is usually given at the same time of antibiotic treatment, prior to CSF analysis and blood culture results. However, the CSF analysis in this question shows evidence of a bacterial meningitis. A viral meningitis would typically be represented by an elevated protein level, normal glucose level and the presence of lymphocytes over polymorphonuclear leucocytes.

Amoxicillin is indicated in treating meningitis in those who are more susceptible to infection with

Listeria monocytogenes

including those over the age of 55 years, pregnant women and the immunocompromised.

Rifampicin and isoniazid are indicated for tuberculous meningitis. However, if tuberculous meningitis is suspected, treatment should include rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for the first 2 months followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for a further 10 months. Tuberculous meningitis is a rare condition and is usually a complication of existing infection with

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

.

Whilst vitamin supplementation, including vitamin C and D is encouraged, it is not recommended in the treatment of bacterial meningitis.

question: A 22-year-old woman who is an immigrant from Malawi presents for review as she thinks she is pregnant. This is confirmed with a positive pregnancy test. She is known to be HIV positive. Which one of the following should NOT be part of the management plan to ensure an optimal outcome?
options: Oral zidovudine for the newborn until 6 weeks of age

question:
A 35-year-old male with a background of HIV presents with a subacute history of headache, vomiting and altered sensation in his right arm. He is known to be poorly compliant with treatment.

Examination reveals hemisensory loss in the right upper limb.

An MRI demonstrates multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white interface. There was minimal mass effect and no midline shift. The images were discussed with the neuro-radiology and neurosurgical teams who felt that a lumbar puncture was safe to perform.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing on the cerebrospinal fluid demonstrates evidence of a parasitic infection.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Immunocompromised patients with toxoplasmosis are treated with pyrimethamine plus sulphadiazine

Pyrimethamine + sulphadiazine is correct and would be the 1st line option for immunocompromised patients requiring treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis.

Clindamycin is incorrect. This would be second-line treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis.

Co-amoxiclav is incorrect. This is not a recognised treatment for toxoplasmosis.

Co-trimoxazole is incorrect. This would be another alternative treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis but would not be the first choice.

No treatment is incorrect. Immunocompromised patients with toxoplasmosis require treatment.

question:
A 33-year-old is investigated for lethargy. The full blood count is reported as follows:


Hb	10.1 g/dl
Plt	156 * 109/l
WBC	3.7 * 109/l

His daughter was unwell one week previously with a pyrexial illness associated with a red rash on her cheeks. What is the most likely cause?

A 31-year-old farm worker visits the GP with a one-week history of profuse watery diarrhoea and a cough. He reports regular fevers and episodes of vomiting too. The patient notes that 3 of his housemates have also developed a similar illness. On examination, he appears clinically dehydrated and has a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. A stool sample has grown Cryptosporidium.

Which stain would confirm this diagnosis?
explanation:
Cryptosporidium can be diagnosed by modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining of stool to reveal red cysts

Cryptosporidium

is a parasite that can cause gastrointestinal and respiratory illness. It is spread by farm animals and contaminated water. A modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain reveals red cysts in the stool of infected individuals, highlighting cryptosporidium oocytes.

Capsule stains are useful to differentiate capsule material from the bacterial cell. These serve the purpose of identifying capsulated bacteria such as

Klebsiella

.

Congo red stain is used to detect amyloid deposits or the cell walls of plants or fungi. It would not aid the identification of

Cryptosporidium

.

Fite's Faraco is a stain used to identify mycobacterium leprae.

Gram stain is used to differentiate gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, with the peptidoglycan wall of positive bacteria appearing purple, and negative bacteria appearing pink. Cryptosporidium would not show up on a gram stain.

question:
You are working in the infectious diseases clinic. A 43-year-old woman with Chagas' disease attends for follow-up. From her records, you note that she has a chronic infection with Trypanosoma cruzi, and is currently receiving benznidazole.

What is the most frequent complication of this infection which you should monitor for?
explanation:
Cardiomyopathy is the most frequent and most severe manifestation of chronic Chagas' disease

Chagas' disease is caused by the  protozoan

Trypanosoma cruzi

. The vast majority of patients (95%) are asymptomatic in the acute phase although a chagoma (an erythematous nodule at site of infection) and periorbital oedema are sometimes seen.

Chronic Chagas' disease mainly affects the heart and gastrointestinal (GI) tract.

GI complications include:

Chronic chagasic megaesophagus: complications include malnutrition, oesophagitis, oesophageal cancer.
Chronic chagasic megacolon: complications include fecaloma, sigmoid volvulus.

The main cardiac complication is chronic chagasic cardiomyopathy, which can lead to congestive heart failure, apical aneurysms and sudden death. This is the most frequent and most severe manifestation of chronic Chagas' disease.

Meningoencephalitis can be seen in African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness).

question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. She returned from a hiking trip in the New Forest 2 weeks ago. On examination, she has a temperature of 38.2°C and a faint circular rash on her thigh. Lumbar puncture shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. Serum ELISA for Borrelia burgdorferi is positive.

What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
IV ceftriaxone should be used as first-line treatment of Lyme disease with disseminated or central nervous system involvement

IV ceftriaxone

is the correct first-line treatment for this patient with Lyme disease with central nervous system involvement. The patient presents with clinical features suggestive of meningitis (headache, neck stiffness, photophobia) and has evidence of CNS involvement with lymphocytic pleocytosis on lumbar puncture. She has a history of potential tick exposure during hiking, a characteristic erythema migrans rash, and positive Borrelia burgdorferi serology. According to UK guidelines, disseminated Lyme disease with neurological involvement (neuroborreliosis) requires intravenous antibiotic therapy, with ceftriaxone being the recommended first-line agent. The typical course is 14-21 days of IV ceftriaxone, which effectively penetrates the blood-brain barrier to treat the CNS infection. This patient's presentation represents a more severe form of Lyme disease requiring parenteral therapy rather than oral options.

Oral amoxicillin

is an appropriate treatment for early, localised Lyme disease, particularly in patients who cannot take doxycycline, such as pregnant women or children under 8 years. However, it is not adequate for CNS involvement as seen in this case. Oral antibiotics do not achieve sufficient CNS penetration to treat neuroborreliosis effectively, making this option inappropriate for this patient with meningeal symptoms and confirmed CSF abnormalities.

Oral doxycycline

is the first-line treatment for early, uncomplicated Lyme disease with erythema migrans but without evidence of dissemination or CNS involvement. While doxycycline does have reasonable CNS penetration compared to some other oral antibiotics, it is still considered insufficient for established neuroborreliosis. This patient's presentation with meningitis symptoms requires more aggressive parenteral therapy.

IV benzylpenicillin

has activity against Borrelia burgdorferi but is not recommended as first-line therapy for neuroborreliosis in UK guidelines. Ceftriaxone has superior CNS penetration and a more convenient once-daily dosing schedule compared to benzylpenicillin, which requires multiple daily doses. While benzylpenicillin could be considered as an alternative in some cases, it is not the optimal first choice.

IV aciclovir

is an antiviral medication used primarily for herpes simplex virus (HSV) or varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infections. While viral meningitis can present similarly to Lyme meningitis, this patient has clear evidence pointing to Lyme disease (erythema migrans rash, positive Borrelia serology, and appropriate exposure history). Aciclovir has no activity against the bacterial spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and would be ineffective in this case.

question:
A 35-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with an itchy rash on his buttocks. He has a past medical history of coeliac disease. He strictly follows a gluten-free diet. He has recently emigrated to the United Kingdom from Catalonia.

On examination, there is an urticarial rash on his buttocks. A similar rash is also noted on his feet. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable.

Urinalysis is unremarkable.

Blood tests:


Hb	144 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	222 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.4 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	4.1 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	1.1 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.4 * 109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.8 * 109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	5.4 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	8 mg/dl	(<5)


What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pruritic rash on the buttocks or soles ?

Strongyloides stercoralis

infection is correct.  This human parasitic disease caused by nematodes is endemic in Catalonia. The urticarial rash on buttock and soles is characteristic, as is blood eosinophilia. Treatment is with ivermectin.

Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. This commonly occurs in association with coeliac disease and affects the buttocks. However, eosinophilia is not typical and the rash is vesicular rather than urticarial. Furthermore, this is less likely to occur in a patient with well-controlled coeliac disease. We are told that he follows a gluten-free diet strictly and there is no history given of disabling gastrointestinal symptoms.

Churg Strauss syndrome is incorrect. This is an eosinophilic multi-system vasculitis that is closely associated with asthma and sino-nasal disease, neither of which are present in this case. Furthermore, an urticarial rash is not typical.

Psoriasis is incorrect. The rash of psoriasis is typically described as red and scaly. Unless the psoriasis was very severe, eosinophilia would not be expected.

Henoch-Schonlein purpura is incorrect. This is a differential diagnosis for a rash on the buttocks but it is purpuric rather than urticarial and is typically associated with either abdominal pain or arthralgia/arthritis.

question:
A 34-year-old farmer presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fevers and bloody diarrhoea. He is passing more than eight bowel motions a day. He reports that he regularly drinks unpasteurised milk.

Given the likely diagnosis, which treatment option is most appropriate?
options: Conservative management without antibiotic treatment or steroids
explanation:
Campylobacter

Clarithromycin is the correct answer. This patient likely has a

Campylobacter

infection given his presentation of bloody diarrhoea, fevers, and consumption of unpasteurised milk.

Campylobacter

infections are typically associated with the consumption of undercooked poultry or unpasteurised milk.

Campylobacter

infection is often self-limiting but if severe then treatment with clarithromycin is indicated. Macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin, clarithromycin, or azithromycin) are the most effective agents for

Campylobacter jejuni

. This patient has a severe infection as he is experiencing fevers, passing more than 8 bowel motions a day, and has bloody diarrhoea.

Ciprofloxacin is an incorrect answer. Ciprofloxacin is an alternative antibiotic to clarithromycin that can be used in the treatment of severe

Campylobacter

infections. However, clarithromycin is the preferred antibiotic as strains with decreased sensitivity to ciprofloxacin are isolated frequently.

Conservative management without antibiotic treatment or steroids is an incorrect answer. Steroids do not have a role in the management of this patient. However, he does require antimicrobial therapy as he has a severe infection.

Hydrocortisone is an incorrect answer. Hydrocortisone is not typically used in the treatment of

Campylobacter

infections. However, it does have a role in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease flares.

Metronidazole is an incorrect answer. Macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin, clarithromycin, or azithromycin) are the most effective agents for

Campylobacter jejuni

. Metronidazole would therefore not be the preferred treatment option in this case.

question: What is the first line antibiotic in the treatment of Shigella dysentery?

A 34-year-old man is found to be HIV-1 positive during a new routine screening programme in the emergency department. He is referred to the sexual health clinic and started on a backbone of dual therapy emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil. Raltegravir is added as a third medication.

What is the mechanism of action of the third medication which has been added?
options: Interferes with the binding, fusion and entry of HIV-1 to the host cell
Acts as a nucleoside analogue which competes with natural deoxynucleotides for incorporation to DNA to prevent reverse transcription
Binds to the reverse transcriptase enzyme to inhibits its function
Blocks integrase enzymatic activity which is involved in inserting the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell
Blocks viral protease enzyme activity necessary to produce mature virions from upon budding from the membrane
correctText: Blocks integrase enzymatic activity which is involved in inserting the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell
explanation:
Integrase inhibitors ('gravirs') - blocks the enzyme that inserts the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell

The correct answer is blocking integrase enzymatic activity. Raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor. There are five classes of medications involved in the treatment of HIV. The NICE guidelines recommend triple therapy for the treatment of HIV. A backbone treatment of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) with an additional third medication. The third medication is recommended to be either an integrase inhibitor (INI), a protease inhibitor (PI) or a non-nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI).

HIV can be targeted at five points in the cell's cycle with drug treatments currently.

Entry inhibitors are a class of medication which

interfere with the binding, fusion and entry of HIV-1 into host cells

. An example of this type of medication includes maraviroc. Maraviroc works by targeting the CCR5 receptor on T-helper cells, reduces the HIV virus' ability to enter the host CD4 cells. Indeed, some individuals may have a mutation of the CCR5 delta gene which results in natural protection from viral cell entry. Nevertheless, caution should be used when administering maraviroc as a tropism of the HIV virus can allow the HIV virus to target an alternative receptor CXCR4 - bypassing maraviroc's mechanism of action.

HIV is an RNA virus and the genetic code be 'reverse' transcribed into DNA in order to be incorporated into the human cell. The conversion of RNA to DNA is not done by mammalian cells and is performed by a viral reverse transcriptase enzyme. This makes it an opportune target for drug therapies. Nulceoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors

act as nucleoside analogues which compete with natural deoxynucleotides for incorporation to DNA to prevent reverse transcription

. Examples of this class of medications include emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil.

Reverse transcription can also be inhibited by non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors. These medications

bind to the reverse transcriptase enzyme and inhibit its function

(acting as allosteric modulators). Examples of this class of medications include efavirenz and nevirapine.

Integrase inhibitors (of which raltegravir is one)

block integrase enzymatic activity which is involved in inserting the viral genome into the DNA of the host cell

. Integrase is a viral enzyme and hence is a reliable target.

Finally, protease inhibitors

block the viral protease enzyme activity necessary to produce mature virions from budding from the membrane

. Viral particles produced in the presence of protease inhibitors are mostly non-infectious and defective. Examples of this class of medications include ritonavir and lopinavir.

question:
A 31-year-old man has presented to the emergency department after his wife was recently discharged from the hospital after receiving treatment for meningococcal meningitis.

He is concerned about being a close contact and was advised that he should commence prophylactic antibiotics.

There are no signs or symptoms of meningitis. He is not on any regular medications and is allergic to penicillin (anaphylaxis). It is decided to start rifampicin as prophylaxis.

What is the mechanism of action?
explanation:
Rifampicin inhibits RNA synthesis

NICE guidelines advice is to offer prophylactic antibiotics to those

'...who have had prolonged close contact with the case in a household-type setting during the 7 days before the onset of illness.'

The BNF advises that ciprofloxacin, rifampicin, or intramuscular ceftriaxone should be used as first-line in the prevention of secondary to meningococcal meningitis.

Rifampicin is a rifamycin antibiotic that acts by

inhibiting RNA synthesis

.

Daptomycin is an example of an antibiotic that

disrupts the cell membrane

and is a treatment option in infective endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections caused by

Staphylococcus

aureus.

Fluoroquinolones, such as ciprofloxacin, act by

inhibiting DNA synthesis

. This antibiotic family is used across a broad spectrum of infections due to its sensitivity to both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms.

Penicillins and cephalosporins act via the

inhibition of cell wall formation

. Like fluoroquinolones, penicillins and cephalosporins can be used for a wide variety of infections as gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria can be treated.

Aminoglycosides, such as gentamicin and streptomycin,

inhibit protein synthesis

and are mostly active against gram-negative organisms, but will treat some infections caused by gram-positive organisms. Aminoglycosides are used mainly in severe infections and as adjuncts alongside other antibiotics. They are poorly absorbed by the gut and are therefore given intravenously, except for neomycin which is used only for skin and mucous membrane infections due to its toxicity.

question:
A 24-year-old refugee from Sudan presents to the Emergency Department with a three-week history of abdominal pain and fevers. She arrived in the United Kingdom one month ago and has been experiencing drenching night sweats during this time.

On examination, there are several areas of hyperpigmented skin on the trunk. There is palpable massive hepatosplenomegaly. The patient's temperature is 38.9ºC and she appears uncomfortable.


Full blood count	Pancytopaenia	
Splenic biopsy	Nonflagellated intracellular amastigotes seen	

What is the most appropriate targeted antimicrobial therapy?
explanation:
Visceral leishmaniasis: sodium stibogluconate is the recommended treatment of choice

Sodium stibugluconate

is the correct answer. Night sweats, massive hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenias, and cutaneous hyperpigmentation in a patient from subsaharan Africa (or India) are concerning for visceral leishmaniasis. Visceral leishmaniasis is caused by

Leishmania donovani

, a protozoan infection spread by sandflies. Diagnosis is confirmed by visualising amastigotes (nonmotile protozoan) on bone or splenic biopsies, though these may be seen on peripheral blood films in patients with high disease burden.

Sodium stibogluconate, an organic antimony derivative, is the treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis. Liposomal amphotericin B is an alternative drug treatment that is preferred in some parts of the world due to local resistance patterns.

Aciclovir

is incorrect. Antiviral therapies are ineffective in visceral leishmaniasis, which is caused by the protozoan

Leishmania donovani

.

Benznidazole

and

nifurtimox

are incorrect. Benznidazole and nifurtimox are antiparasitic agents used to treat Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis. There is no role for benznidazole or nifurtimox in the management of visceral leishmaniasis.

Doxycycline

is incorrect. Conventional antibiotics are ineffective in treating visceral leishmaniasis caused by the protozoan

Leishmania donovani

.

question:
A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for review and stool sample results. He has now had diarrhoea for 13 days, passing watery stool up to ten times per day with some flecks of blood. He is drinking well but feels tired and feverish.

On examination, he appears tired with dry mucous membranes. His heart rate is 110bpm, blood pressure 124/78mmHg, and temperature 37.8ºC. His stool sample is positive for campylobacter.

What would be the most appropriate first-line treatment?
explanation:
Campylobacter

Campylobacter

is usually a self-limiting infection, but antibiotics are indicated if patients are immunocompromised or if it is severe (multiple episodes loose stool, bloody diarrhoea, fever). In this case, the prolonged duration with profuse diarrhoea and fever would indicate starting antibiotics. If antibiotics are used they should be clarithromycin or azithromycin.

Co-amoxiclav is a broad spectrum antibiotic suitable to treat diverticulitis. Caution is needed with co-amoxiclav as it can cause

clostridium difficile

infection.

Cefotaxime can be used to treat

typhoid

or severe

salmonella

infections, but not

campylobacter

infections.

Metronidazole is a useful antibiotic for anaerobic infections, it can be used for

clostridium difficile

infections.

Vancomycin is second-line treatment for

clostridium difficile

.

question:
A 45-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a three-month history of rash and abnormal sensation in his lower limbs. He has no significant past medical history other than a raised body mass index (BMI) of 35 kg/m² and being of tall stature (1.9 metres). He is on no regular medications. He is originally from India and arrived in the United Kingdom six months previously. He smokes shisha regularly with his friends.

On examination, there were 2-3 hypopigmented patches on his lower limbs. Neurological examination reveals reduced sensation in a glove and stocking distribution with hair loss. The common fibular nerve was thickened and palpable in the right lateral popliteal fossa.

Blood tests:



Hb	136 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7.9 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.4 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	89 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	4 mg/L	(< 5)
HbA1c	54 mmol/mol	(<48)


What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberculoid leprosy is suggested by a limited number of skin lesions, hypaesthesia and hair loss

Tuberculoid leprosy is the correct answer. This patient presents with a recent onset of hypopigmented skin lesions, sensory peripheral neuropathy and thickened peripheral nerves having come from an endemic region.

Acromegaly is incorrect. While this disorder can cause thickened peripheral nerves, it is a less likely cause of skin lesions a sensory neuropathy. While we are told he is of tall stature, there is no suggestion that there are any coarsening of his facial features, enlargement of his extremities or any other typical features of this condition.

Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. While this condition can cause thickened peripheral nerves (due to tumour growth along nerves) and is associated with skin lesions in the form of cafe au lait spots, it is an inherited condition that tends to develop over many years, rather than being of subacute onset in later life.

Type 2 diabetes is incorrect. While this patient appears to have developed diabetes, based on his HbA1c result, the constellation of findings favours leprosy rather than diabetes. Thickened peripheral nerves are not a typical feature of diabetes nor are patches of hypopigmented skin. Diabetic patients can get a rash on their shins (Necrobiosis lipoidica) but this is typically an erythematous rash that may ulcerate if injured.

question:
A 19-year-old student attends the general medical clinic. She has returned from Mozambique recently and have noticed new urinary symptoms. Of note, they developed a rash while in Mozambique after they went swimming. The rash gradually resolved but since returning they have had blood in their urine and are micturating with greater frequency.

What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Schistosomiasis is treated with praziquantel

Schistosoma haematobium

is one species of the parasitic trematode fluke species termed Schistosoma.

Schistosoma haematobium

is one of two species endemic in Africa which may induce schistosomiasis. This particular species is known to induce urinary symptoms similar to a urinary tract infection. The most common presenting features are haematuria, increased frequency, suprapubic discomfort, and burning pain on passing urine. If left untreated, the infection can cause fibrosis and will predispose infected patients to squamous cell carcinoma. It can also affect the genital organs leading to vaginal bleeding in women or haematospermia in men.

The diagnosis is made on history followed by microscopy showing viable eggs. Molecular techniques may also be employed as necessary.

The definitive treatment for infection is with praziquantel.

Doxycycline is an anti-malarial as is quinine.

Artemisinin has been used along with praziquantel for treatment of schistosomiasis but would not be a sole agent or first line.

Ciprofloxacin is used for the treatment of pyelonephritis.

question:
A 36-year-old male is seen in hepatology outpatients with a repeat hepatitis screen. He describes a 1-week history of anorexia, fatigue and jaundice. On examination there was no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease, JVP 3cm, mild scleral icterus, abdomen was soft, non-tender, with 2cm regular liver edge.

Key:


HBs Ag	Hepatitis B surface antigen
HBe Ag	Hepatitis B E antigen
HB DNA	Hepatitis B DNA titre
Anti-HBs	Anti Hepatitis B surface antibody
Anti-HBc IgM	Anti Hepatitis B core antibody
Anti-HD IgM	Anti Hepatitis D IgM antibody

Bloods: 6 months ago


HBs Ag	positive
HBe Ag	positive
HB DNA	positive
Anti HBs	negative
Anti HBc IgM	positive
Anti HD IgM	negative

Bloods: Today


HBs Ag	positive
HBe Ag	positive
HB DNA	positive
Anti HBs	negative
Anti HBc IgM	positive
Anti HD IgM	positive
