question:
A 26-year-old patient presents with bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fever. Prior to this he felt unwell for a couple of days with malaise and headache. He returned 3 days ago from a holiday in Morocco, where he ate mostly food cooked by street vendors.

On examination, he has generalised abdominal tenderness, worst in the right iliac fossa.

What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Campylobacter infection is characterised by a prodrome, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea

The correct answer is

Campylobacter

, a known cause of gastroenteritis, especially after foreign travel. Several factors point to

Campylobacter

being the correct answer, including bloody diarrhoea, prodromal symptoms and abdominal pain mimicking appendicitis. The incubation period is unclear in this case.

Campylobacter

is associated with foreign travel and eating undercooked poultry, consistent with the patient's history.

Amoebiasis

is caused by

Entamoeba histolytica

and is spread via faeco-oral transmission. It is common in developing countries and can cause a spectrum of diseases, from asymptomatic to profuse, bloody diarrhoea. It typically has a subacute onset - over one to three weeks - and is less associated with prodromal symptoms of malaise and headaches. The prodromal symptoms in this case, along with the acute onset of disease mimicking appendicitis, make

Campylobacter

infection more likely.

E. coli

is the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the returning traveller, but it is uncommon to cause bloody diarrhoea - making it an unlikely cause in this case.

Giardiasis

is a caused by the protozoan

Giardia lamblia

and is spread via faeco-oral transmission. It tends to cause prolonged non-bloody diarrhoea, bloating and flatulence rather than the symptoms in this case.

Whipple's disease

is a rare multi-system condition caused by the bacterium

Tropheryma whipplei

. It will cause diarrhoea, but it is unlikely to cause bloody diarrhoea. It is also likely associated with other symptoms, including arthralgia and lymphadenopathy.

question:
A 33-year-old man who injects heroin presents with a 3-day history of left-sided groin swelling at a recent injection site. On examination, there is a large area of black skin discolouration and a sinus with purulent discharge. He is tachycardic and pyrexial. Blood tests reveal raised inflammatory markers. He is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and referred for surgical debridement of the site. Blood cultures subsequently reveal aerobic gram-positive bacilli.

Which antibiotic is most likely to be suitable for ongoing treatment?
explanation:
Anthrax presents with a black eschar that is typically painless; it is treated with ciprofloxacin

Intravenous drug use may cause acute skin infection, often caused by Streptococcal or Staphylococcal species (both gram-positive cocci). Rarely, heroin may be contaminated with

Bacillus anthracis

or

Clostridia

species, including

C. botulinum

,

C. perfringens

and

C. novyi

.

Bacillus anthracis

(anthrax) is a spore-forming, aerobic gram-positive bacillus.

Clostridia

species are also spore-forming gram-positive bacilli but they are anaerobic. Cutaneous anthrax may present with a black eschar lesion (differentials for this include Rickettsia). In a review of UK cases of anthrax associated with intravenous drug use, eschar was not always present. Although treatment would be based on sensitivities, cutaneous anthrax is typically treated with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline.

Clindamycin is useful for Staphylococcal bone and joint infections such as osteomyelitis, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

Daptomycin may be used for complicated skin and soft-tissue infections caused by gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA. Like vancomycin, it does act against gram-negative bacteria. Due to its activity against gram-positive bacteria, it may be an alternative antibiotic depending on sensitivities but it is not the first-line choice in the treatment of anthrax.

Flucloxacillin is useful against Infections due to beta-lactamase-producing staphylococci. It has a role in the treatment of skin infections including impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas, diabetic foot infections, infected leg ulcers and osteomyelitis. It is not the first-line choice in the treatment of anthrax.

Vancomycin may also be used for complicated skin and soft-tissue infections caused by gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA. It does not act against gram-negative bacteria. Due to its activity against gram-positive bacteria, it may be an alternative antibiotic depending on sensitivities but it is not the first-line choice in the treatment of anthrax.

question:
A 34-year-old lady presents to the GP with worsening nausea and fatigue over a 2 week period. On examination, there is a yellow tinge to the sclera of her eyes. She lives in a remote fishing village and consumes a diet high in seafood. She does not smoke or consume alcohol. She does not report any weight loss or other constitutional features. Her LFTs are as follows:


Bilirubin	20 µmol/l
ALP	160 u/l
ALT	550 u/l
Î³GT	30 u/l
Albumin	35 g/l

Other routine blood results are within normal limits.

What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

There has been a recent outbreak of norovirus in a local nursing home. The manager of the care home has contacted you at the GP surgery seeking information on this illness and advice on how to reduce the risk of spreading the virus.

Which of the following is the most appropriate advice on preventing the spread of this virus?
options: Handwashing with soaps and warm water before and after contact with those infected with norovirus
Regular use of alcohol gels before and after contact with those infected with norovirus
Early treatments with antivirals in suspected cases of norovirus
Avoid contact with any blood products of those infected with norovirus
Staffs infected with norovirus should only return to work 24 hours after symptoms have resolved
correctText: Handwashing with soaps and warm water before and after contact with those infected with norovirus
explanation:
Alcohol gels are less effective than handwashing in preventing the spread of norovirus

The correct answer is 'handwashing with soaps and warm water before and after contact with those infected with norovirus'. Alcohol gels are less effective than handwashing in preventing the spread of norovirus.

There are no roles of antivirals in the treatment of norovirus.

Norovirus is not a blood-borne virus. They are commonly spread through contaminated food or drinks, touching surfaces or objects contaminated with norovirus or having direct contact with someone who is infected with norovirus.

Staffs infected with norovirus must stay off work for at least 48 hours after symptoms have stopped.

question: Following a recent holiday to South America, a 19-year-old woman returned home and within a month developed a swelling around the right cheek with increased fatigue and diarrhoea. Diagnostic thick and thin blood films identified the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. Which medication can be used to treat her condition during the acute phase of the disease?
explanation:
Benznidazole is used in the acute phase of Chagas' disease to manage the illness

Azoles such as benznidazole are antifungal medications which target the p450 cytochrome enzyme system to inhibit the growth of a wide range of organisms.

Riluzole - used to manage motor neurone disease

Praziquantel - used in patients with schistosomiasis

Miltefosine - Used in patients with Leishmaniasis

Chloroquine - Used in the treatment of Malaria

question:
A 25-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a two-day history of jaundice. She is 12 weeks pregnant and has no other past medical history. She denies diarrhoea or vomiting but did admit to attending a barbecue two weeks before, where she had concerns about how thoroughly the meat had been cooked.

Her blood test results are shown below:


Hb	120 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	70 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	12.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Bilirubin	87 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	150 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	581 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	62 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	37 g/L	(35 - 50)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Haemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome
explanation:
Severe hepatitis in a pregnant woman - think hepatitis E

The correct answer is

hepatitis E infection

. This patient has severe transaminitis in the first trimester of pregnancy. This should make candidates consider hepatitis E infection, as pregnant patients tend to experience a more severe course of infection than other patient groups. Additional factors supporting the diagnosis of hepatitis E infection include thrombocytopenia, which is a recognised extra-hepatic manifestation of this infection, and the history of recent attendance at a barbecue (hepatitis E is often contracted from undercooked pork).

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

is incorrect. This is very unlikely to present at 12 weeks gestation. It tends to present towards the end of the third trimester, with an average onset of around 36 weeks gestation.

Haemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome

is incorrect. This is a complication of pre-eclampsia which almost universally presents in the third trimester or immediately after delivery, rather than at 12 weeks gestation. Questions referring to HELLP syndrome will normally include other indicators of pre-eclampsia, such as proteinuria or hypertension.

Hepatitis A infection

is incorrect. This tends to be transmitted by shellfish rather than undercooked pork. It is also much less likely to cause severe disease in pregnant patients than hepatitis E and is not typically associated with thrombocytopenia.

Pregnancy induced cholestasis

is incorrect. It is more likely to present towards the end of pregnancy and classically manifests as pruritus (itching), which is not present in this case.

question:
A 32-year-old woman is seen in the sexual health clinic. She has a 3-day history of dysuria and vaginal discharge. Her past medical history includes migraines and asthma. She takes sumatriptan and a fluticasone inhaler and has no known drug allergies.

A vulvovaginal swab is taken and tested using nucleic acid amplification. This confirms a diagnosis of Chlamydia trachomatis.

What is the most appropriate antibiotic to start?
explanation:
Chlamydia

Doxycycline

is now the first-line treatment for

Chlamydia

. Previously, azithromycin was used, but due to increasing rates of coinfection with

Mycoplasma genitalium,

, which has rising levels of macrolide resistance, doxycycline is now the first line recommended therapy.

Amoxicillin

is used to treat many infections, including chest and urinary infections. It may be used in the treatment of

Chlamydia

in pregnancy, where doxycycline is contraindicated. However, azithromycin would still be preferred in pregnancy in these circumstances. In non-pregnant patients the drug of choice remains doxycycline.

Azithromycin

is one option that may be used if doxycycline is contraindicated, such as in pregnancy. However, doxycycline is preferred as a first-line treatment due to concerns about

Mycoplasma genitalium

, which often coexists in patients with chlamydia and shows rising levels of macrolide resistance.

Ceftriaxone

is used as the first-line treatment for gonorrhoeal infection, not chlamydia. It is given as a single intramuscular dose.

Ciprofloxacin

is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic. It has no role in the treatment of chlamydia infection.

question:
A previously healthy 33-year-old male attends the emergency department with fever and severe joint pain affecting several different joints at different times over the past few days, currently worst in the right knee, as well as pain along the Achille's tendon. He also noticed a new skin rash on his chest.

Examination finds significant limitation in range of movement of the right knee due to pain. Several small macules are visible on the patient's chest.

Synovial fluid cultures are negative.

What is the most likely underlying infection?
explanation:
Disseminated gonococcal infection triad = tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthritis, dermatitis

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

can disseminate and cause the typical triad of dermatitis, migratory polyarthritis, and tenosynovitis. This is an exam favourite. The tendon and joint involvement are thought to be due to immune complex deposition, which results in an inflammatory response. They typically yield negative synovial fluid and joint cultures and rarely leads to significant joint destruction. The rash typically affects the trunk, limbs, palms and soles, and usually spares the face, scalp and mouth. This patient's joint pains and tendon pain coupled with the skin rash make this the most likely diagnosis.

Candida albicans

doesn't tend to cause disseminated disease in immunocompetent individuals. It can cause septicemia, which may also manifest with skin lesions and arthralgia, in immunocompromised patients. There is no mention of risk factors for immunosuppression, such as steroid use or HIV.

Chlamydia trachomatis

can cause Sexually Acquired Reactive Arthritis (SARA) and is not at all an unreasonable option and often catches candidates out in exams. However, it is less likely to cause migratory polyarteritis specifically and dermatitis, which are typical features of disseminated gonococcal infection.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) will not usually cause a macular skin rash but typically an itchy blistering one instead, usually near the mouth or genitals. The description of skin rashes is an important piece of knowledge for systemic conditions with dermatological features. Fever, lymphadenopathy and a widespread rash would be the features of disseminated HSV infection.

Trichomonas vaginalis

can (rarely) cause systemic complications such as pneumonia but is not the most likely cause of this patient's constellation of signs and symptoms.

question:
A 7-year-old unvaccinated child is brought into the emergency department after having returned from a family holiday in South-East Asia. The child initially developed a sore throat and fevers 3 days ago which has progressed to a severe, harsh cough.

On examination, a covering can be seen on the posterior aspect of the child's throat and he has enlargement of cervical lymph nodes.

Throat swab cultures confirm a gram-positive bacterium and treatment is initiated with intramuscular penicillin and antitoxin.

What sequela is most associated with this infection?
explanation:
One of the sequelae of diphtheria is cardiovascular disease; notably heart block

This child has presented with features in keeping with diphtheria caused by the gram-positive bacteria

Corynebacterium diphtheriae

. Initially, patients commonly manifest with a sore throat and fevers, which later progress to a severe cough resembling that of croup. One characteristic indication of the condition is the presence of a grey pseudomembrane on the back of the pharyngeal wall, referred to as a 'diphtheric membrane'. Diphtheria is known to be linked with various sequelae, and one well-established consequence of the infection is the development of atrioventricular

heart blocks

. These heart blocks may present several years after the initial infection has occurred.

Glomerulonephritis

is a common complication of various infections, with

Streptococcus pyogenes

being the most frequent causative agent. This complication is believed to arise due to the formation of immune complexes during the infection, which get deposited in the glomeruli and trigger an inflammatory response. Although renal damage can result from exotoxins released in diphtheria infections, these typically cause tubulointerstitial nephritis and not glomerulonephritis.

Mitral valvular disease

is a common feature of rheumatic fever, an inflammatory disease that occurs post-streptococcal throat infection. While myocarditis has been linked to diphtheria, there is no clear association between the infection and mitral valvular disease.

Splenomegaly

can be a consequence of various infectious conditions, often due to the enlargement of lymphatic tissue. Common infections that can lead to splenomegaly include infectious mononucleosis (caused by the Epstein-Barr virus), cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, and malaria. Diphtheria is not typically associated with splenomegaly.

Subconjunctival haemorrhage

can occur as a result of intense coughing, but only a few infections lead to such severe coughing.

Bordetella pertussis

, which causes pertussis, commonly known as whooping cough, is one such infection. Although the cough associated with diphtheria may mimic that of croup, it is rarely severe enough to result in subconjunctival haemorrhage.

question:
A 32-year-old man has 3 months of fever, weight loss, night sweats, and abdominal distention. He recently returned from a 6-month trip in rural India and recalls being bitten by flies.

His temperature is 38.5ºC and has marked hepatosplenomegaly, but no lymphadenopathy. He is cachectic, with ashen, grey skin, bruising over his lower limbs, and pale conjunctivae.

Investigations:


Hb	93 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	95 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	3.1 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Splenic biopsy	amastigotes within macrophages

Which option is the most likely route of infection?
explanation:
Leishmaniasis is caused by the intracellular protozoa

Sandfly bites

is correct. This 32-year-old man presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, night sweats, cachexia, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopaenia, and greyish skin, following travel to rural India. These features are classic for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), caused by

Leishmania donovani

. The diagnosis is confirmed by amastigotes within macrophages on splenic biopsy. This protozoan parasite is transmitted by infected female phlebotomine sandflies, making sandfly bites the most likely route of infection.

Aedes mosquito bites

is incorrect because they transmit arboviruses such as dengue and chikungunya, which do not cause the clinical or laboratory findings seen here. Dengue typically presents with acute high fever, myalgia, rash, and bleeding, while chikungunya causes fever and joint pain. Neither causes prolonged illness with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, or amastigotes within macrophages. These infections would be considered if the patient had an acute febrile illness with rash or arthralgia following travel to endemic areas, which does not apply here.

Culex mosquito bites

is incorrect because they are associated with Japanese encephalitis and lymphatic filariasis, neither of which matches this patient’s symptoms or biopsy findings. Japanese encephalitis presents with fever, altered mental status, and seizures, while filariasis causes chronic lymphoedema and elephantiasis. This patient has none of these features and instead shows signs of a chronic systemic protozoal infection with hepatosplenomegaly and intracellular amastigotes, which rules out

Culex

-transmitted infections.

Female blackfly bites

is incorrect because they transmit

Onchocerca volvulus

, causing onchocerciasis (river blindness), which presents with chronic pruritus, skin nodules, depigmentation, and visual impairment. This patient has none of those features. Instead, he shows signs of visceral involvement, pancytopenia, and splenic amastigotes, which are not seen in onchocerciasis. Also, onchocerciasis typically follows travel to Africa or parts of Latin America, not rural India.

Tsetse fly bites

is incorrect because they transmit

Trypanosoma brucei

, the cause of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), which presents with intermittent fever, lymphadenopathy (notably posterior cervical 'Winterbottom’s sign'), and progressive neurological decline. This patient lacks these features and instead has massive hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and splenic amastigotes, all consistent with visceral leishmaniasis. Moreover, tsetse flies are found in sub-Saharan Africa, not India.

question: A 19-year-old man presents with an annular rash, pyrexia and polyarthralgia to the Emergency Department. He has just returned from the New Forest and remembers being bitten by a tick. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
explanation:
First line treatment for early Lyme disease is a 14-21 day course of oral doxycycline

As he only has features of early disease, doxycycline is sufficient.

question:
A 26-year-old male presents with a 24-hour history of abrupt onset headache, fever, nausea and vomiting, fatigue and photophobia. He has no medical history.

On examination, he has nuchal rigidity and Kernig's sign was positive. He is alert and orientated. He has a heart rate of 106/min, respiratory rate of 18/min, blood pressure 136/86 mmHg, and a temperature of 38.2 ºC.

Investigations:


Hb	140 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	390 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	12.1 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	7.0 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	5.0 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)


CT Head	Normal

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF):


Opening Pressure	18 cm³ H²O	(10 - 20)
Cell count	200 cells/µL (Lymphocytes)	(0 - 5)
Glucose	3.6 mmol/L	( 2.8 - 4.2)
Protein	0.8 g/dL	(0.15 - 0.45)
Gram stain	No organisms seen

Which organism is the most likely cause of this patient's illness?
explanation:
The most common causes of viral meningitis in adults are enteroviruses

This is a typical presentation of viral meningitis, the most common cause of which is the non-polio enteroviruses (e.g. Coxsackie virus, Echovirus). The presence of headache, with nausea and vomiting, along with examination findings of nuchal rigidity (inability to flex the neck / reduced range of motion of the neck), Kernig's sign (hip and knee flexed to 90º and then the extension of the knee cause pain), and Brudzinski's sign (forced flexion of knee causes reflex flexion of hips) all point towards meningism. The findings of the lumbar puncture are typical for 'aseptic meningitis' of which enteroviruses are the most common cause.

Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus: this is a rodent-borne arenavirus and infection is usually linked to exposure to their urine and stool. This is unlikely given this patients occupational background.

Mumps: before the arrival of vaccinations, Mumps was a very common cause of aseptic/viral meningitis; however, this is no longer the case. Furthermore, this individual received his childhood vaccinations making this even more unlikely.

Neisseria meningitidis

: the lumbar puncture findings are certainly not typical of a bacterial infection. If it were

Neisseria meningitidis

causing meningitis, you would expect a low CSF glucose, neutrophil predominance and high protein, and gram-negative diplococci on gram stain.

Herpes simplex virus type 1: this usually causes viral encephalitis (HSV-2 generally causes more viral meningitis). Furthermore, HSV-related meningitis is more likely to occur with primary infections and this individual has no evidence of primary HSV infection (oral/genital ulcers); it is much less common in those with asymptomatic primary HSV infections. An HSV encephalitis typically presents with altered mental status and/or behavioural changes.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the sexual health clinic with a two-day history of white vaginal discharge. She reports that the discharge has been offensive and fishy-smelling. She reports that she is sexually active currently, and has had two sexual partners in the last three months.

On examination, she is found to have a homogenous white discharge which is foul-smelling. The pH is found to be 6.1.

The sample is sent for microscopy and culture.

What type of organism would be expected to be seen on under the microscope?
explanation:
Bacterial vaginosis - overgrowth of predominately

The patient has presented with a typical history of bacterial vaginosis. There is a white homogenous discharge which is foul-smelling. Bacterial vaginosis occurs where there is an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria, leading to a loss of lactic acid-producing lactobacilli. This leads to a rise in pH to above 4.5.  Whilst bacterial vaginosis is not a sexually transmitted infection. It is more commonly seen in people who are sexually active. The most commonly seen organism is

Gardnerella vaginalis

a peptidoglycan walled coccobacillus which can appear as both gram-positive or occasionally gram-negative due to its very thin wall.

Gram-negative diplococci would represent

Neisseria gonorrhoea

in a question about vaginal discharge. Whilst the patient is sexually active there are more pointers to suggest that this is bacterial vaginosis. Gonorrhoea infection would not change the pH in this way.

Intracellular gram-negative bacteria are suggestive of

Chlamydia trachomatis

. As above whilst the patient is stated to be sexually active. The history is more typical of bacterial vaginosis.

Lactobacilli make up the lactic acid-producing bacteria that normally lower the vaginal pH. These are the cells which would be seen less or absent under the microscope in bacterial vaginosis.

Yeast cells would be seen in a

Candida albicans

infection. Typically candida infections manifest with vaginal itching and a thicker and less homogenous white discharge.

question: Which one of the following organisms causes lymphogranuloma venereum?
explanation:
Lymphogranuloma venereum -

Chlamydia

is the correct answer, specifically serovars L1, L2, or L3 of

Chlamydia trachomatis

. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by these invasive serovars of

Chlamydia trachomatis

. Unlike the more common urogenital serovars (D-K) that typically cause urethritis or cervicitis, the LGV serovars have a predilection for lymphatic tissue. The infection typically presents in three stages: a primary stage with a painless papule or ulcer at the site of inoculation that often goes unnoticed; a secondary stage characterised by painful inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (often unilateral), which may suppurate forming buboes; and a tertiary stage that can lead to genital elephantiasis, fistulae, and strictures if left untreated. In recent years, there has been an increase in LGV proctitis among men who have sex with men in the UK and Europe. Treatment typically involves doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 21 days.

Haemophilus ducreyi

is incorrect. This gram-negative coccobacillus is the causative agent of chancroid, another sexually transmitted infection. Chancroid presents as a painful genital ulcer with a ragged edge and a purulent base, often accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. Unlike LGV, the ulcers of chancroid are typically painful from the outset. The lymph nodes may suppurate but do not typically develop the fibrosis and chronic inflammation seen in LGV.

Klebsiella granulomatis

(formerly known as

Calymmatobacterium granulomatis

) is incorrect. This bacterium causes donovanosis (granuloma inguinale), a sexually transmitted infection characterised by painless, progressive ulcerative lesions on the genitals or perineal area. The lesions are beefy red and bleed easily on contact. Unlike LGV, donovanosis does not typically cause significant lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is made by identifying Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusions) in tissue smears.

Herpes simplex virus

is incorrect. HSV, particularly HSV-2, causes genital herpes, which presents with painful vesicular lesions that ulcerate. While HSV can cause lymphadenopathy, it does not cause the characteristic buboes or chronic lymphatic obstruction seen in LGV. HSV infections are also typically recurrent, whereas LGV is not.

Treponema pallidum

is incorrect. This spirochaete is the causative agent of syphilis. Primary syphilis presents with a painless, clean-based ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation, which may be accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy. However, the lymphadenopathy in syphilis is typically non-suppurative and painless, unlike the often painful, suppurative lymphadenopathy seen in LGV. Additionally, syphilis progresses through distinct secondary and tertiary stages with different clinical manifestations from those seen in LGV.

question:
A 19-year-old medical student undergoes primary immunisation against hepatitis B. Following the full cource of vaccines, his post immunisation bloods are reported as follows:


Anti-HBs	< 10 mIU/ml

What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Give one further dose of hepatitis B vaccine
Test for current or past hepatitis B + repeat course (i.e. 3 doses) of vaccine
Give two further doses of hepatitis B vaccine
Give a course of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) + one further dose of hepatitis B vaccine
correctText: Test for current or past hepatitis B + repeat course (i.e. 3 doses) of vaccine

question: A 40-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit following a severe episode of acute pancreatitis. On the third day of his admission he becomes pyrexial. A septic screen is ordered including cultures taken from both peripheral blood and the internal jugular line. There is no signs of infection on the chest x-ray or urine sample. The microbiology laboratory phone to report signs of bacterial infection in the sample from the central line. What is the most likely organism to be isolated?
explanation:
Most common organism found in central line infections -

The correct answer in this scenario is

Staphylococcus epidermidis

. The reason for this is that

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is a common cause of central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI). It is part of the normal skin flora and can easily contaminate the insertion site or hub of a central venous catheter, leading to infection. In this case, the patient has no signs of infection on chest x-ray or urine sample, and the bacterial growth was detected in the sample from the internal jugular line, making it more likely to be related to the central line.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

is an incorrect answer as it is less commonly associated with CLABSI compared to

Staphylococcus epidermidis

. Although

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

can cause nosocomial infections, it typically affects patients with compromised immune systems or those with chronic lung diseases such as cystic fibrosis.

Escherichia coli

is also an incorrect answer. While

E. coli

can be a cause of bloodstream infections, it usually originates from urinary or gastrointestinal sources rather than central lines. In this case, there are no signs of infection in the urine sample which makes it less likely.

Streptococcus pneumoniae

is not the correct answer because it primarily causes community-acquired pneumonia and meningitis rather than CLABSI. Additionally, there are no signs of infection on chest x-ray in this patient, making it less likely to be caused by

S. pneumoniae

.

Finally,

Staphylococcus aureus

is an incorrect answer, although it is a more common cause of CLABSI compared to other options like

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

,

Escherichia coli

, and

Streptococcus pneumoniae

. However,

Staphylococcus epidermidis

remains the most likely organism to be isolated in this scenario due to its prevalence as a causative agent for CLABSI.

question:
A 56-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit following a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Over the course of a week, she shows general improvement. Today, however, she spikes a fever twice and is noticeably hypotensive, which is not responding to an intravenous fluid bolus. Some purulent discharge is noted around the site of her central line.

What is the most likely cause of this patient's sudden deterioration?
explanation:
Most common organism found in central line infections -

The most likely culprit is

Staphylococcus epidermidis

. This patient's clinical picture is suggestive of a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI).

Staphylococcus epidermidis

, a coagulase-negative staphylococci, is a common cause of CLABSI. These organisms are part of the normal skin flora and can contaminate intravascular catheters leading to biofilm formation. The presence of fever, hypotension and purulent discharge around the central line site in this patient strongly suggests a central line infection.

Although

Staphylococcus aureus

could also cause such an infection,

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is more commonly associated with device-related infections. Other listed organisms are less likely in this scenario.

Candida albicans

has been reported to cause CLABSI, particularly in specific population groups such as patients receiving a high glucose concentration through intravenous hyperalimentation and immunosuppressed patients who have been administered multiple antibacterial drugs. Since the patient in the case scenario does not fall into these categories,

Candida

infection is unlikely.

Pseudomonas species

are a rare cause of CLABSI. However, it is the most frequent isolate in bloodstream infection (BSI) seen in patients with burns. Gram-negative pathogens like

E.coli

and

Pseudomonas

species predominate in BSI occurring in patients with malignancies. However, given that the patient does not fall into these specific groups of patients,

Pseudomonas

species are an unlikely cause.

Streptococcus pyogenes

is not a pathogen that is commonly described as causing CLABSI.

Streptococcus pyogenes

is the most common cause of bacterial pharyngitis in children and adolescents. Less commonly,

Streptococcus pyogenes

causes invasive skin infections leading to bacteraemia and necrosis of soft tissues.

question:
A 24-year-old man presents to his GP with diarrhoea.

He has just returned from a week in Morocco.

Starting on the last day of his holiday, he described watery diarrhoea 4-5 times per day. He describes some mild cramping pains in his abdomen and nausea, but no vomiting. There is no blood in the stool.

He is afebrile and his observations are all normal.

Abdominal examination is unremarkable.

What is the most likely cause of this man's diarrhoea?
explanation:
E. coli

Escherichia coli

is correct. This patient is experiencing traveller's diarrhoea. The most common cause of this is

Escherichia coli

.

Salmonella typhi

is incorrect. This is the organism responsible for typhoid fever. This patient does not have typhoid fever; this would be characterised by a high fever accompanied by abdominal pain, constipation and vomiting. Diarrhoea is unusual.

Shigella

is incorrect.

Shigella

produces prolonged, bloody diarrhoea and fevers.

Staphylococcus aureus

is incorrect. This produces severe vomiting, followed by watery diarrhoea. Vomiting is not a feature in this patient, so this answer is incorrect.

Vibrio cholerae

is incorrect. This is the organism that produces cholera. Cholera is characterised by severe watery diarrhoea resulting in dehydration and systemic upset. This is not described in this case, making

Vibrio cholerae

incorrect.

question:
A 55-year-old man presents to the GP with haemoptysis, fever, and night sweats. He has travelled monthly to India for business over the past two years. His medical history includes COPD, and he received the BCG vaccine.

On examination, he has tender cervical lymphadenopathy and his chest is clear on auscultation. He is euvolaemic with a temperature of 39.8 ºC.

The following blood tests are conducted:


Na+	128 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.1 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	23 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	5.6 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	98 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

A chest x-ray reveals consolidation in the right upper lobe.

What is the most likely infecting organism?
explanation:
The BCG vaccine is unreliable in protecting against pulmonary tuberculosis

The patient has presented with classical clinical features of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), including haemoptysis, night sweats, fever, and lymphadenopathy. He has a history of travel to India, a country with a high incidence of TB. Other manifestations may include dyspnoea and weight loss. Although auscultation of the chest may be unremarkable as in our patient's case, crepitations or bronchial breathing might also be detected. The patient exhibits hyponatraemia, which is likely secondary to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), a condition commonly associated with pulmonary TB. Radiological evidence from the chest x-ray reveals consolidation within the right upper lobe, further supporting the diagnosis of pulmonary TB. Despite previous BCG vaccination, this does not preclude a TB diagnosis since its protection against pulmonary TB is not reliably effective. Consequently, the most probable causative organism is

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

.

Haemophilus influenzae

is frequently identified in infective exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Nevertheless, such exacerbations would not typically present with haemoptysis and would more likely demonstrate wheezing on examination. Considering the patient’s recent travel history to India and their symptomatology, pulmonary TB remains a more plausible diagnosis.

Klebsiella pneumoniae

infection can produce bloodstained sputum often likened to 'red currant jelly', yet it is not classically associated with night sweats or international travel. It predominantly occurs in individuals who consume excessive alcohol and can lead to cavitating lung lesions—neither of which apply to this case.

Legionella pneumophila

, while often encountered in travellers due to its presence in warm water systems and air conditioning units, presents differently. Although it could cause hyponatraemia via SIADH similarly to our case, the symptoms of haemoptysis and night sweats are less indicative of Legionnaires’ disease. Features such as upper lobe consolidation on imaging and clear lung fields upon auscultation may occur in Legionnaires’ disease but are more characteristic of TB.

Infection with

HIV

can lead to an acute flu-like illness during seroconversion approximately 1-2 weeks post-infection. While India has a higher prevalence of HIV compared to the United Kingdom—and it is indeed an MRCP favourite scenario for describing a businessman returning from overseas with HIV—the current clinical picture does not align with seroconversion; the severity of illness here is too great and includes signs and symptoms such as haemoptysis, night sweats, and upper lobe consolidation that are atypical for seroconversion. Moreover, this presentation does not correspond with opportunistic infection by

Pneumocystis jirovecii

, which typically manifests with exertional dyspnoea and a diffuse ground-glass appearance on chest x-ray.

question:
An HIV positive patient presents for his regular clinic check-up having started antiretrovirals a few months previously. He is well and has an undetectable viral load on Truvada (emtricitabine/tenofovir) and raltegravir.

His blood tests are unremarkable apart from having a CD4 count of 184 cells/mm³.

Which drug should be added to his prescription for preventive purposes?
explanation:
All patients with a CD4 count lower than 200/mm

All patients with a CD4 count lower than 200 cells/mm³ should receive prophylaxis against

Pneumocystis jirovecii

pneumonia.

Aciclovir is sometimes used as longterm herpes suppression treatment in patients with both HIV and HSV.

The other answers are not routinely used as prophylaxis.

question:
A 32-year-old HIV-positive gentleman has been on treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in the form of co-trimoxazole. He reported initially experiencing some improvement in his breathing but more recently became very breathless when walking short distances. He felt his breathing was quite noisy at times too.

The patient reported taking his medication regularly and eventual persistence with treatment led to a resolution in his symptoms. He was reviewed at the HIV clinic where he was subsequently started on aerosolized pentamidine as prophylaxis treatment. Now having been on this treatment for 6 months he presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of difficulty in breathing.

What is the likely cause of this acute presentation?
explanation:
Aerosolized pentamidine is an alternative treatment for

Aerosolized pentamidine prophylaxis for

Pneumocystis jirovecii

pneumonia in patients with the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) may often not be effective. Bullous changes and pulmonary cysts can form in lung apices from repetitive inflammation and cytotoxicity of HIV on the pulmonary macrophages. These changes persist in spite of prophylaxis against recurring pneumocystis infection with aerosolized pentamidine which increases the risk of spontaneous pneumothorax.

Given the acute presentation, it is less likely to be community-acquired pneumonia or empyema.

Empyema is a collection of pus in the pleural cavity which can result in fevers, chest pain, difficulty in breathing and productive coughing. This is most commonly caused by pneumonia but can be due to tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, chest surgery and trauma.

Flail chest occurs due to trauma where a rib cage segment is broken and becomes completely detached from the chest wall resulting in chest pain and difficulty in breathing.

Whilst these patients can get reactivation of latent TB, this would present with other symptoms such as fevers, chills, night sweats, cough and even haemoptysis in severe cases.

question: A 27-year-old woman attends the hospital occupational health clinic prior to starting work on a haematology ward. She has no significant medical history and her vaccinations are up to date except for MMR and varicella, both of which are recommended. According to UK guidelines, how should these vaccines be scheduled if given by injection?
options: Give both at the same visit or ≥4 weeks apart
Administer with a minimum interval of 1 week
Give MMR first, then varicella after 2 weeks
No specific scheduling required for live vaccines
correctText: Give both at the same visit or ≥4 weeks apart
explanation:
Live vaccines given by injection may be either given concomitantly or a minimum interval of 4 weeks apart to prevent risk of immunological interference

Give both at the same visit or ≥4 weeks apart

: This is correct. UK guidelines state that injectable live vaccines (such as MMR and varicella) can either be administered concomitantly (on the same day) or, if not given together, must be spaced by a minimum of 4 weeks. Giving them too close together but on different days may result in immunological interference, potentially reducing vaccine efficacy. This principle applies specifically to live parenteral vaccines.

Administer with a minimum interval of 1 week

: A one-week interval is insufficient between two injectable live vaccines not administered simultaneously. Studies have shown that shorter intervals may lead to suboptimal immune responses due to interference between the attenuated viruses.

Give MMR first, then varicella after 2 weeks

: Two weeks is still too short an interval for separate administration of injectable live vaccines according to UK and international guidance. The recommended gap is at least four weeks if they are not given together.

Separate by at least 6 months

: There is no requirement for such a prolonged interval between injectable live vaccines; this would unnecessarily delay full immunisation and leave the individual susceptible for longer than necessary.

No specific scheduling required for live vaccines

: This statement is incorrect as there are clear recommendations regarding timing when administering multiple injectable live-attenuated vaccines. Failure to adhere could compromise vaccine effectiveness.

question: A 74-year-old woman has a chest x-ray organised by her GP due to a chronic cough. The chest x-ray shows a cavity in the left upper zone inside of which there is a solid mass. An aspergilloma is suspected. What is the most appropriate next test?

A newly qualified staff nurse at the local hospital undergoes vaccination against hepatitis B. The following results are obtained three months after completion of the primary course:


Result	Anti-HBs: 10 - 100 mIU/ml
Reference	An antibody level of >100 mIU/ml indicates a good immune response with protective immunity

What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Repeat course (i.e. 3 doses) of hepatitis B vaccine
Repeat anti-HBs level in three months time
Give a course of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) + one further dose of hepatitis B vaccine
Give one further dose of hepatitis B vaccine
correctText: Give one further dose of hepatitis B vaccine

question:
A 25-year-old woman has recently moved to the United Kingdom from sub-Saharan Africa to attend University. She comes from an area where there is a high prevalence of tuberculosis (TB). The patient is not pregnant and is currently asymptomatic. She thinks she may have had a BCG vaccination in the past but is not sure. She has no other medical history and is a non-smoker. A chest x-ray is normal. She has a Mantoux test which is positive and subsequently an interferon-gamma release assay which is also positive.

What is the best management option for this patient?
options: Rifampicin and isoniazid with pyridoxine for 6 months
Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 6 months

question: A 25-year-old intravenous drug user with chronic hepatitis C becomes pregnant. Approximately what is the chance of the virus being transmitted to her child?

A 48 year old farmer attends the emergency department 7 days after cutting his arm from falling on barbed wire in his field. He complaints of fever, headache and painful spasms in his neck and back which last several minutes.

You suspect tetanus and he tells you he has completed a course of tetanus vaccination previously.

What is the most appropriate treatment?
Which one of the following conditions is not associated with prior Epstein-Barr virus infection?
explanation:
EBV: associated malignancies:

Adult T-cell leukaemia is associated with HTLV-1 infection

question:
A 19-year-old man presents with a 12-hour history of a headache and fever. On examination, you elicit neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign. He scores 15 on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and there has been no change in behaviour and there is no evidence of raised intracranial pressure. He is haemodynamically stable and there is no rash.

Blood cultures are taken and a lumbar puncture is performed. You decide to treat empirically for bacterial meningitis and prescribe intravenous cefotaxime every 6 hours.

Which of the following is most appropriate in addition to intravenous cefotaxime?
options: Give intravenous dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose and continue every 6 hours
Give intravenous dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose only
Await the cerebrospinal fluid results and prescribe intravenous dexamethasone only if Streptococcus pneumoniae is isolated
correctText: Give intravenous dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose and continue every 6 hours
explanation:
Dexamethasone improves outcomes (by reducing neurological sequelae) in the treatment of bacterial meningitis

1: Aciclovir should be given if herpes simplex encephalitis is suspected, based on reduced consciousness or change in behaviour or cognition. These features are not present and so aciclovir is not indicated.

2: This is the correct answer. Intravenous dexamethasone should be given prior to or with the first dose of antibiotic to reduce the risk of neurological sequelae by reducing cerebrospinal inflammation. If pneumococcal meningitis is suspected or confirmed from clinical features, cerebrospinal fluid parameters or culture results, then dexamethasone should be continued for 4 days. It should be stopped if another causative organism is strongly suspected or confirmed.

3: Dexamethasone should be continued until investigation results suggest an alternative organism to

Streptococcus pneumoniae

.

4: Dexamethasone should be given with the first dose of antibiotic to reduce the risk of neurological sequelae.

5: Amoxicillin is recommended in addition to cefotaxime in the empirical treatment of patients <3 months old or >50 years old.

question: A 63-year-old man who migrated from India 7 months ago is referred to the acute medical unit with a history of headache and pyrexia. A lumbar puncture suggests a diagnosis of meningeal tuberculosis. What treatment should he be started on?
options: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and streptomycin
Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol with prednisolone
correctText: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol with prednisolone

question:
A 44-year-old woman attends with a one-week history of a productive cough and shortness of breath. She recently was diagnosed with influenza A. She keeps a parrot as a pet. Observations are as follows: heart rate 115 beats per minute, blood pressure 135/80 mmHg, temperature 38.6ºC, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 92% on air.

A chest x-ray was performed:


Chest x-ray	Right-sided lobar pneumonia with evidence of cavitation

What organism is most likely implicated?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus

Staphylococcus aureus

is correct. Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent cause of secondary bacterial pneumonia following influenza A infection. The presence of cavitating lesions adds further weight to this diagnosis.

Chlamydia psittaci

is incorrect. Psittacosis is an infection of birds caused by the bacterium

C. psittaci

. The disease has been described in many species of birds, particularly in parrots, parakeets, budgerigars and cockatiels. It typically causes flu-like symptoms (fever, headache, muscle aches) but can lead to severe pneumonia. The pneumonia is usually atypical with perihilar patchy reticular or reticulonodular opacities. The presence of lobar pneumonia and cavitation, in this case, makes psittacosis an unlikely diagnosis. Although she keeps a parrot as a pet, it is important to look at the overall picture.

Coxiella burnetii

is incorrect. Q fever is a disease caused by the bacteria

Coxiella burnetii

. This bacteria naturally infects some animals, such as goats, sheep, and cattle. The most common manifestation is flu-like symptoms however it can progress to an atypical pneumonia.  The presence of lobar pneumonia and cavitation, in this case, makes Q fever an unlikely diagnosis.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae

is incorrect. This pathogen presents with a flu-like illness, atypical pneumonia, and red cell agglutination on blood film analysis. The agglutination of red cells can result in haemolytic anaemia. The presence of lobar pneumonia and cavitation, in this case, makes

Mycoplasma pneumoniae

an unlikely diagnosis.

Varicella zoster virus

is incorrect. Varicella pneumonia is the most common and serious complication of chickenpox infection in adults. Secondary bacterial infections can also occur. The classic chest X-ray appearances are of multiple 5-10 mm ill-defined nodules that may be confluent and fleeting.  The chest x-ray appearances and absence of a rash, in this case, make Varicella pneumonia an unlikely diagnosis.

question: Which one of the following vaccines uses a protein that attaches to the polysaccharide outer coat to make the pathogen more immunogenic?

A 27-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a blurred vision, slurred speech and weakness of both her arms. She reports that these symptoms started the previous day and has attended now as she is having difficulty swallowing. She denies any past medical history, or current medications.

On examination, the patient is unkempt. You note multiple track marks on both arms. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the cranial nerves reveals a bilateral ptosis. The patient reports diplopia bilaterally and there is impaired pupil accommodation. The gag reflex is impaired, and the patient's speech is slurred. Examination of the upper limbs reveals hypotonia, hyporeflexia and power is 3/5 bilaterally. Sensation is intact. Examination of the lower limbs is unremarkable.

You suspect the patient may have an infection with clostridium botulinum, and send blood samples for clostridium botulinum toxin.

What is the next most appropriate step in management?
options: Await serum clostridium botulinum toxin results
explanation:
The treatment of botulism - supportive care and botulism antitoxin

The clinical syndrome produced by botulinum toxin is an afebrile, descending, flaccid paralysis. Presenting features typically include difficulty speaking or slurred speech, blurred or double vision, and/or dysphagia. Other features include ptosis and facial muscle weakness. Without treatment, paralysis may progress to the upper limbs, trunk, lower limbs and respiratory muscles.

Intravenous drug users are particularly at risk of developing infection with clostridium botulinum, through injecting contaminated drugs into skin or muscle. Botulism spores are found naturally in the environment (such as in soil), so they can contaminate supplies of drugs such as heroin.

If botulism is suspected, swift administration of botulism antitoxin is essential in order to reduce the severity of symptoms, therefore this is the next most appropriate step in management of this patient.

Public Health England recommend that in cases where there is clinical suspicion of botulism, treatment with antitoxin should not be delayed for microbiological testing.

Supportive care, including serial measurements of forced vital capacity, is also essential, however on its own this is not the correct answer.

Clostridium botulinum

is sensitive to benzylpenicillin, and therefore this is also administered in patients with abscess formation at the injection site. However, this is not the most essential step in management.

Tetanus immunoglobulin is used in the management of tetanus, caused by

clostridium tetani

.

question:
A 25-year-old female primary school teacher presents to the emergency department with a rash and fever. She states that there have been a number of cases of slap cheek (parvovirus B19) infection at the school.

Of the choices given, what is the most important consideration?
explanation:
Parvovirus is a common cause of fetal hydrops during pregnancy and can be treated with fetal transfusion

'Erythema infectiosum', 'fifth disease' and 'slap cheek' are the same condition which are all possible manifestations of parvovirus B19 infection. It is associated with fetal abnormalities and commonly causes a characteristic rash in children and in adults in can additionally cause arthralgia.

Infection in a pregnant woman can lead to fetal hydrops and spontaneous miscarriage, particularly in the first trimester. This can be managed with the use of fetal blood transfusion.

In patients with sick-cell disease, aplastic crisis may be precipitated by parvovirus. Immunocompromised individuals are also at risk.

question:
A 35-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department with fever and hypotension. He had returned 2 days previously from a business trip from India, which lasted 3 weeks. The patient had not sought any pre-travel advice and had not taken any malaria prophylaxis.

The patient was pale and looked lethargic. His temperature was 38.5ºC, oxygen saturations were 92% on air, blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg and heart rate was 135/min at initial presentation.

A malaria rapid diagnostic kit had revealed a probable falciparum malaria.

Which of the following options is most appropriate?
explanation:
Quinine is no longer recommended as a first-line treatment for complicated/severe falciparum malaria

Whilst all the above options are potential antimalarial treatments, according to the UK malaria treatment guidelines 2016 (Journal of Infection) IV artesunate is the first line treatment where available for complicated or severe malaria.

The patient is shocked and this therefore suggests complicated malaria.

Several trials have demonstrated benefit of IV artesunate over IV quinine for complicated falciparum malaria.

question: A 44-year-old farmer presents with headache, fever and muscle aches. He initially thought he had a bad cold but his symptoms have got progressively worse over the past week. During the review of systems he reports nausea and a decreased urine output. On examination his temperature is 38.2ºC, pulse 102 / min and his chest is clear. Subconjunctival haemorrhages are noted but there is no evidence of jaundice. What is the most likely diagnosis?

You are phoned for advice. The parents of a 19-year-old man have just been messaged by their son who is currently backpacking in Thailand. Earlier in the day he was bitten by a dog whilst staying in a rural community. Prior to travelling, he received vaccination against rabies as he was going to be visiting many rural areas. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: He should increase his fluid intake by around 1L a day as a precaution
He should be protected given the previous vaccination but should monitor for any changes in salivation over the next 72 hours
He should see a local doctor to request antibiotic therapy
He should urgently seek local medical attention for consideration of booster vaccination + antibiotic therapy
He should take the next flight home so he can be observed for any symptoms of rabies
correctText: He should urgently seek local medical attention for consideration of booster vaccination + antibiotic therapy

question: A man presents with severe vomiting. He reports not being able to keep fluids down for the past 12 hours. You suspect a diagnosis of gastroenteritis and on discussing possible causes he mentions reheating curry with rice the night before. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Bacillus cereus

The correct answer is

Bacillus cereus

. This gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium is commonly associated with food poisoning from improperly stored and reheated rice dishes. The organism produces two types of toxins: an emetic toxin that causes vomiting (predominant symptom occurring 1-5 hours after ingestion) and a diarrhoeal toxin. The spores can survive cooking and, if rice is left at room temperature, they can germinate, multiply and produce toxins. Reheating does not destroy these pre-formed toxins.

Escherichia coli

typically causes food poisoning through contaminated meat products or unwashed vegetables. The incubation period is usually longer (12-72 hours), and diarrhoea is the predominant symptom rather than vomiting. While it can cause severe illness, it would be less likely in this scenario involving reheated rice.

Campylobacter

is commonly associated with undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk, and contaminated water. It typically has a longer incubation period (2-5 days) and presents with diarrhoea, often bloody, along with severe abdominal pain and fever. The presentation and food history in this case do not fit with Campylobacter infection.

Salmonella

infection typically occurs through contaminated eggs, poultry, or dairy products. The incubation period is usually 12-72 hours, and symptoms include diarrhoea, fever, and abdominal cramps. The rapid onset of predominantly vomiting symptoms and the association with reheated rice makes Salmonella less likely.

Shigella

is transmitted through the faecal-oral route and is commonly associated with poor hygiene rather than reheated food. It typically causes dysentery with bloody diarrhoea, fever, and abdominal pain, with an incubation period of 1-7 days. The clinical presentation and food history make this an unlikely causative organism in this case.

question:
A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of intermittent fevers and fatigue. He is normally fit and well and takes no regular medication. He has no recent travel history but is concerned about some undercooked meat he recently ate at a friend's house.

On examination, his temperature 37.6ºC, heart rate 82bpm, blood pressure 128/78mmHg. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, the chest is clear and the heart sounds normal. He has some cervical lymphadenopathy but normal tympanic membranes. The oral mucosa appears normal.

Blood tests reveal a mild lymphocytosis and his Toxoplasmosis serology is positive.

What would be the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Immunocompetent patients with toxoplasmosis don't usually require treatment

Supportive care with fluids and analgesia is correct. Most infections caused by

Toxoplasma gondii

are self-limiting, and treatment is not necessary for immunocompetent people. Exceptions include patients with eye involvement (toxoplasma chorioretinitis) and those who are immunosuppressed such as in acquired immunodeficiency (AIDS).

Amphotericin can be used to treat visceral leishmaniasis.

Metronidazole is the treatment for

Giardia lamblia

and amoebic infections.

If treatment is required for toxoplasmosis infection such as toxoplasmic encephalitis related to AIDS then a combination of pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine is usually given for several weeks.

Spiramycin may reduce the risk of

toxoplasmosis

transmission from mother to fetus in pregnancy.

question:
A 25-year-old enters the emergency department after an altercation. He explains that he got into a fight with another person while drunk in a pub. Although his memory is hazy he remembers being punched in the face and being bitten on his hand.

On examination, there is extensive bruising around the left orbit and a bite mark on the lateral surface of the left hand.

Which of the following antibiotics should be prescribed for the bite?
explanation:
Human bites, like animal bites, should be treated with co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav would adequately cover the main organisms implicated in a human bite. This includes

Streptococcus

,

Staphylococcus

,

Eikenella

,

Corynebacterium

and other anaerobes. Even if there are no signs of infection antibiotics should be prescribed.

Metronidazole with clarithromycin (or doxycycline) can be used and is generally reserved for patients who are penicillin-allergic. This should also be avoided in this particular patient as a disulfiram-like reaction may occur due to his intoxication.

Doxycycline alone can be used if other medications are not available but will not be as effective.

Amoxicillin would not cover the β-lactamase producing bacteria.

question:
A 25-year-old man has been admitted to hospital with several injuries after he was mugged on his way home from the pub last night. During the altercation, he was bitten by his attacker and has been left with deep bite marks on his hand, which looks red and swollen. You prescribe tetanus and hepatitis B prophylaxis.

Which antibiotic will you prescribe for him?
options: Await swab results and discuss with microbiology before deciding if an antibiotic is necessary
explanation:
Human bites, like animal bites, should be treated with co-amoxiclav

Doxycycline and metronidazole are an acceptable treatment of human bites if the patient is penicillin-allergic, however as this is not stated we assume that he has no allergies.

Co-amoxiclav is the correct answer.

Awaiting the swab results is not the correct answer. Human bites like animal bites are treated with co-amoxiclav. Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for: hand/foot/facial injuries, deep puncture wounds or wounds requiring surgical debridement, wounds involving joints/tendons/ligaments, suspected fractures, and in patients who are immunosuppressed, diabetic, cirrhotic, asplenic, or elderly. Antibiotic treatment is required for bites which look infected. In this case, the bite both appears infected (red, swollen), and is on the hand so would require antibiotics regardless of infection.

Flucloxacillin is the treatment for cellulitis.

Clindamycin and ciprofloxacin are used in the treatment of severe human bites if penicillin-allergic.

question:
Kasim is a 45-year-old man who has recently immigrated to the UK from Pakistan. He is seeking medical attention as he has noted several unsightly lesions along his forearm. These lesions have been growing over the past 4 months.

On examination, you see a total of 3 lesions over his left forearm. These are raised and erythematous. He noticed that when you touch the lesions, he is unable to feel you touching it. This is confirmed when he denies any fine touch or pin-prick sensation on the lesion. There is significant hair loss overlying the lesion. A tender cord-like structure is palpable close to the medial epicondyle. The right forearm remains unaffected.

There are no other significant systemic symptoms.

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberculoid leprosy is suggested by a limited number of skin lesions, hypaesthesia and hair loss

The presence of hypoesthesia with raised lesions along the arm raises the suspicion of leprosy as the underlying diagnosis. This is further evidenced by the presence of thickened cord-like structures that are tender, likely representing inflamed nerve fibres involved in the disease.

Tuberculoid leprosy is the preferred answer as this patient has limited skin lesions with the accompanying hypoesthesia. Accompanying thickened and tender nerves also contribute towards this diagnosis.

Lepromatous leprosy tends to be more systemic with widespread involvement of the skin forming nodules. This can also be associated with the leonine facies ( thickened forehead with loss of eyebrows and eyelashes). Associated systemic symptoms include hepatitis, orchitis, uveitis and corneal anaesthesia.

Pityriasis versicolor is a yeast infection driven by the genus

Malassezia

and can be associated with hypo-pigmented lesions. However, this does not result in reduced sensations or thickened nerve fibres.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis are caused by the

Leishmania

parasite and are transmitted by sandflies. Raised lesions can be found but this is normally accompanied by a degree of central ulceration. Hypoesthesia is not a feature in this.

Yaws is a tropical disease caused by

Treponema palladium pertenue

and usually presents as a single lesions on the skin with associated lymphadenopathy. This is erythematous and often accompanied by a yellow crust on the surface. There is usually no accompanying sensory changes.

question:
A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a history of confusion, severe malaise, vomiting, fever and a 'sunburn like' rash involving her upper body, palms, soles and lips.

She is normally fit and well. Her only past medical history of note is menorrhagia; she has been referred by her GP to gynaecology regarding this. She takes tranexamic acid as required. She recently returned from a holiday in Ibiza.

On examination, she is pyrexial, hypotensive, and has diffuse macular erythroderma with red oral mucosa. Glasgow coma scale 14/15, her neurological examination is normal. Her chest is clear and abdomen is non-tender.

Initial blood tests find elevated creatinine kinase, an elevated creatinine level and deranged liver function tests.

Blood cultures are positive for Staphylococcus aureus.

Other microbiological tests are negative including serology for rickettsia, leptospirosis, and measles.

Which of the following factors is most likely to be contributory to this patient's presentation?
explanation:
Tampon use is a risk factor for staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome

The stem is describing toxic shock syndrome secondary to

Staphylococcus aureus

infection.

Tampon use is a major risk factor for this illness; particularly the use of tampons for prolonged periods of time.

Pneumonia and skin infections are also associated with toxic shock syndrome but are less likely in this case are there are no signs of them on clinical examination.

Foreign travel and alcohol consumption are not linked to toxic shock syndrome.

question: Which one of the following statements best describes the prevention and treatment of hepatitis C?
options: No vaccine is available and treatment is only successful in around 10-15% of patients
No vaccine and no treatment is available
A vaccine is available and treatment is successful in around 50% of patients
A vaccine is available but no treatment has been shown to be effective
No vaccine is available but treatment is successful in the majority of patients

question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman is found to have Chlamydia. She reports being allergic to penicillin. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Azithromycin, erythromycin or amoxicillin may be used to treat

The BNF recommends azithromycin, erythromycin or amoxicillin for pregnant women who have

Chlamydia

.

The efficacy of amoxicillin, often assumed to be ineffective against

Chlamydia

, was supported in a recent Cochrane review. A test of cure should be carried out following treatment.

question:
A 25-year-old man presents with worsening sore throat, fever, and a painful swelling near the angle of his jaw. He has difficulty opening his mouth and complains of neck pain on the same side. Two days later, he develops shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain.

Chest imaging reveals multiple cavitating pulmonary nodules. Blood cultures grow anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Deep neck space cellulitis with septic emboli
Infective endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli
Necrotising fasciitis of the neck with septic emboli
explanation:
Patients with peritonsillar abscesses can develop Lemierre's syndrome (thrombophlebitis of the IJV)- this can present with neck pain, and can result in septic pulmonary embolism

Peritonsillar abscess with septic emboli

is the correct answer.  Peritonsillar abscess often follows a bacterial sore throat, most commonly caused by

Streptococcus pyogenes

(Group A Streptococcus), while

Fusobacterium necrophorum

, an anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus, is particularly associated with Lemierre’s syndrome rather than peritonsillar abscess in general. The infection can spread laterally from the abscess and compress the adjacent internal jugular vein (IJV), leading to thrombophlebitis, known as Lemierre’s syndrome, which specifically refers to thrombophlebitis of the IJV leading to septic emboli, not just any case of peritonsillar abscess with embolic complications. Patients typically present initially with a sore throat, then develop neck pain, stiffness, and tenderness, which can mimic meningitis, along with systemic symptoms such as fevers and rigors. The pathophysiology involves infected thrombus formation in the IJV, which then acts as a nidus for septic emboli that disseminate, most notably to the lungs, causing cavitating pulmonary nodules, as seen in this patient.

Deep neck space cellulitis with septic emboli

is incorrect because deep neck space cellulitis causes neck swelling and pain, but less commonly leads to septic emboli. The presence of cavitating pulmonary nodules and positive blood cultures for anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli is more characteristic of abscess formation with embolic spread rather than cellulitis alone. The clinical signs of trismus and focal swelling suggest abscess rather than cellulitis.

Infective endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli

is not the correct answer. While infective endocarditis can cause septic emboli, left-sided endocarditis typically causes systemic emboli, and pulmonary septic emboli more commonly arise from right-sided endocarditis, often associated with intravenous drug use. However, the clinical picture described does not fit this scenario, as there are no cardiac symptoms or a relevant history provided. Neck pain and localised swelling near the jaw are not features of infective endocarditis. The Gram-negative anaerobic bacteria isolated are uncommon pathogens in endocarditis.

Necrotising fasciitis of the neck with septic emboli

is unlikely as necrotising fasciitis often involves mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria (polymicrobial infection), presents with rapidly progressive soft tissue destruction, severe systemic toxicity, and often overt local necrosis.  Anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli, such as

Bacteroides

species, may occasionally be involved in necrotising fasciitis. It is less likely to cause septic emboli with cavitating pulmonary nodules without severe local signs. This patient’s clinical course and examination findings are more in keeping with an abscess complicated by embolic spread rather than necrotising fasciitis.

Disseminated gonococcal infection

is incorrect. While it can present with systemic symptoms, migratory polyarthritis, tenosynovitis, and even pulmonary involvement in rare cases, it typically does not present with a sore throat, neck swelling, or cavitating pulmonary nodules. Blood cultures in disseminated gonococcal infection may not always yield

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

, and it is not associated with anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli. The clinical picture here, particularly with internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis and septic pulmonary emboli, is more characteristic of Lemierre’s syndrome.

question:
A 23-year-old solider who returned from a tour of Afghanistan 2 months ago presents with a large painless ulcer on the back of his hand. He reports that it started as a small papule and gradually enlarged. On examination he has a 3cm ulcer with a central depression and a raised indurated border. He is otherwise well in himself and has no other medical problems.

What is the likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old man who is taking immunosuppressive therapy for Adult onset Still's disease, and has come into contact with a child who has chicken pox. He is varicella zoster IgG antibody negative. He has a small number of early chicken pox blisters and you decide to start aciclovir therapy.

Which of the following fits best with the mode of action of aciclovir?
explanation:
Aciclovir is much more specific for viral than mammalian DNA polymerase

Aciclovir is phosphorylated after entry into herpes infected cells to form aciclovir triphosphate. The first step in this process is dependant on the presence of HSV-coded thymidine kinase. Aciclovir triphosphate acts as an inhibitor of, and substrate for, the herpes-specific DNA polymerase, preventing further viral DNA synthesis without affecting normal cellular processes. It is 10-30 times more specific for viral DNA polymerase versus the human enzyme.

Bacterial DNA gyrase is the target of quinolone antibiotics. Reverse transcriptase is an enzyme target for the treatment of RNA viruses such as HIV. NS3/4A and NS5A are both targets in the treatment of hepatitis C. Modern antivirals which target NS3/4A and NS5A have revolutionised the treatment of hepatitis C, bringing cure into focus for the first time.

https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/5692/smpc#PHARMACODYNAMICPROPS

Serum glucose	4.9 mmol/l

Lumbar puncture reveals:


Opening pressure	14 cmCSF	(10 - 20 cmCSF)
